Source data                        ICAM4 is highly expressed in erythroid cells (Supplementary Fig.  8c ). ICAM4 level increases during the early stages of human terminal erythropoiesis (CD235a + CD71 + ), followed by a moderate decline in the late stage (CD235a + CD71 med ) (Supplementary Fig.  9 ). These findings suggest that ICAM4 may facilitate the formation and cohesion of erythroid islands during early differentiation, while its downregulation at later stages may promote the release of mature erythroid cells from the niche. To test the function of ICAM4, we applied the iPS cell-derived human bone marrow organoid model and treated the organoids with antibodies against ICAM4. Flow cytometry assays revealed that anti-ICAM4, but not anti-RHAG or control IgG, significantly reduced the number of CD71 + /CD235a +  erythroid cells (Fig.  6b,d ) without affecting their differentiation (Fig.  6c,e ). A confocal imaging assay further showed that blocking ICAM4 significantly reduced the number and size of macrophage-independent EBIs (>5 cells per cluster) (Fig.  6f  and Supplementary Fig.  10a ).  ICAM4 was reported to interact with macrophage α v -integrin in mouse macrophage-centered EBIs  41  . To exclude the remote possibility that the disrupted EBIs were a result of macrophage–erythroid interactions, we performed an in vitro colony-forming unit assay using a medium containing only Epo, which differentiates the human CD34 +  HSPCs exclusively into erythroid lineages. Consistent with the organoid data, we found a significant reduction in erythroid colonies when HSPCs cultured in Epo medium were treated with anti-ICAM4. By contrast, cells treated with IgG, anti-RHAG or anti-α v -integrin showed no changes in erythroid island formation (Fig.  6g,h ). These findings support that ICAM4 is critical for the formation of macrophage-independent EBIs in humans. Interestingly, the level of ICAM4 was significantly reduced in the erythroblasts from the bone marrow of patients with MDS compared to those from healthy individuals (Fig.  6i,j  and Supplementary Fig.  10b ), which further suggests that the compromised integrity of macrophage-independent EBIs by reduced ICAM4 expression could be a dysplastic feature of MDS.     Discussion  Our study reveals fundamental species differences in EBI anatomy and molecular mechanisms. In mice, canonical macrophage-centered EBIs persist throughout development, with C1q serving as a hallmark of the central macrophage. C1q, a component of the classical complement pathway, facilitates macrophage phagocytosis by binding phosphatidylserine exposed on pyrenocyte surfaces following erythroid enucleation. Notably, erythrocytes express C1q receptors (CR1/CD35) that block complement opsonization  42  . Whether pyrenocytes exhibit reduced receptor expression warrants future investigation. In addition to phagocytosis, C1q regulates MerTK expression on macrophages to promote nuclear clearance  43   and limits inflammasome activity during apoptotic cell uptake  44  , both of which are critical for maintaining bone marrow homeostasis. Collectively, these functions align with known EBI macrophage roles in mice, supporting C1q as a key marker of macrophage heterogeneity.  In contrast to mice, human hematopoietic tissues are predominantly composed of macrophage-independent erythroid clusters. Although macrophage-centered EBIs are critical for mouse erythropoiesis, human erythroid maturation exhibits far greater spatial autonomy. Conventional macrophage-centered EBIs do occur in humans but are rare and stochastic. We found that ICAM4 is critical for the integrity of human EBIs. ICAM4 is an erythroid-specific glycoprotein originally identified as the LW blood group antigen and subsequently classified among the intercellular adhesion molecules  45  . ICAM4 interacts with different integrins, including CD11a/CD18 (LFA-1)  45 , 46  , CD11b/CD18 (Mac-1)  46  , CD11c/CD18 (ref.   47  ) and α v -integrin  48  . However, these surface proteins are predominantly expressed in leukocytes. Before this study, the mechanisms by which ICAM4 mediates spatial organization among human erythroid progenitors were unknown. We demonstrate that ICAM4 is essential for human EBI integrity and erythroid proliferation. Parallel ligand–receptor analysis in mouse fetal liver identified canonical macrophage–erythroid interaction pairs, consistent with macrophage-centered murine organization. Together, these findings suggest that species-specific differences in intercellular adhesion programs underlie the divergent erythroid niche architectures in mice and humans, potentially reflecting upstream differences in transcriptional regulation by master erythroid regulators such as GATA1, KLF1 or TAL1, which require further investigation.  Notably, macrophage-independent erythroid clusters are also prevalent in mouse hematopoietic tissues. Spatial transcriptomic data reveal that erythroid–erythroid spatial correlation indices exceed those between erythroid cells and C1q +  macrophages, suggesting that erythroid clustering is a conserved feature of the erythropoietic niche. Evolutionarily, macrophage-centered EBIs appear to have diminished in humans, becoming rare and stochastic. This architectural divergence may partly reflect differences in the extracellular matrix: in mice, fibronectin and laminin support erythroid adhesion and terminal differentiation  2  , potentially stabilizing macrophage-centered EBIs, whereas human bone marrow, characterized by greater adiposity and reduced cellularity  39 , 49 , 50  , may impose different spatial constraints that reduce reliance on macrophage anchoring. Together, species-specific variation in extracellular matrix composition and adhesion molecule programs probably shapes the divergent erythroid clustering strategies observed across species, warranting further investigation.  Although human macrophages are not anatomically integrated into EBIs, they may perform analogous functions in a paracrine manner, including pyrenocyte phagocytosis and nutrient supply to erythroid cells. C1Q +  macrophages in human bone marrow may also compensate for EBI defects in LW-null individuals. The predominance of macrophage-independent erythroid clustering in both species raises important questions about pyrenocyte clearance, such as whether other phagocytes are involved, and whether alternative clearance mechanisms exist beyond macrophage phagocytosis. This study provides a framework for addressing these questions.    Methods   Mouse sample collection  All animal studies followed the Guidelines for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at Northwestern University (protocol number IS00033835). Wild-type (C57BL/6) mice used in Visium and Xenium spatial transcriptomic assays were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. C1qa knockout mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (cat. no. 031675). EpoR-tdTomato-Cre mice were kindly provided by X. An from the New York Blood Center. The following timing protocol was used for the collection of embryonic stage and postnatal stage samples: one male and one female mouse per cage were mated in the afternoon of day 1 and separated in the morning of day 2. Subsequently, all female mice were individually housed in new cages and marked as pregnant at 0.5 days after mating.  For fetal liver sample collection, post-mating pregnant mice were killed, and the fetal livers of a specific embryonic stage were collected. For postnatal sample collection, mice on postnatal day 8 were used for bone marrow collection. For spleen collection, normal spleens were collected from wild-type mice at 2 months old. For spleens from PHZ-treated mice, 40 mg kg −1  PHZ or vehicle (1× PBS) was injected intraperitoneally twice daily for 2 days. Then, PHZ-treated and control mice were killed, and spleens were collected. The selected tissues for spatial transcriptomics in this study are representative of at least ten independent biological replicates per condition and reflect normal physiological states or defined experimental conditions.  All freshly collected samples were directly fixed in a 10% neutral buffered formalin solution (Sigma-Aldrich) and kept at room temperature (20 °C to 22 °C) for 3 days. Mouse sample embedding and sectioning were performed at the Mouse Histology and Phenotyping Laboratory facility, Northwestern University.    Human sample collection  Human bone marrow aspirate samples, clot sections and core biopsy blocks were obtained from leftover diagnostic specimens at Northwestern Memorial Hospital. No written consents from patients were required for this study, given that the samples were part of the routine diagnostic materials. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Northwestern University (IRB ID STU00217116). Human sample embedding and sectioning were performed at the Pathology Core Facility, Northwestern University.    Visium spatial transcriptomics  Visium whole transcriptome spatial RNA sequencing platforms (Visium V1) for mice and humans were purchased from 10x Genomics. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks were used for the spatial analyses. To confirm the RNA quality of each FFPE block, one to two curls (10 μm thickness each) of the block were tested using a Qiagen RNeasy FFPE kit (Qiagen, 73504) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Extracted RNAs were examined using an Agilent Bioanalyzer RNA pico chip to confirm DV200 > 30%. Simultaneously, the tissue morphology was examined using H&E stain to identify the region of interest.  For each FFPE sample, 5 µm sections were placed on Visium slides (four capture areas of 6.5 mm × 6.5 mm each; smaller tissues were co-placed in a single area). Slides were incubated at 42 °C for 3 h, followed by overnight room temperature incubation, then stored in a desiccated chamber until deparaffinization. Deparaffinization, decrosslinking, probe hybridization and ligation were performed using the 10x Genomics FFPE Visium spatial gene expression kit (v2 probes; PN-1000188; protocols  CG000409  and  CG000407 ). Probes were released, captured and extended on the Visium slide, and sequencing libraries were prepared per the manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 S2 flow cell (100 cycles; 28 nt read 1, 90 nt read 2) at the NUSeq Core, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.    Xenium spatial transcriptomics  Xenium transcriptome spatial RNA sequencing platforms for mice and humans were purchased from 10x Genomics. As with the Visium procedure, 5 μm-thick sections were placed on the Xenium slide capture area, followed by 3 h of 42 °C incubation and overnight drying. Slides were stored at room temperature in a desiccation chamber until proceeding to deparaffinization.  Slide processing and Xenium analyzer loading were carried out using Xenium slide and sample prep reagent kit (PN1000460), Xenium decoding consumables (PN-1000487) and Xenium decoding reagent (PN-1000461). Slides were first deparaffinized and de-crosslinked according to the manufacturer’s protocol ( CG000580 ). Then, custom probes with pre-designed panel genes were hybridized to the sample slide overnight, followed by probe ligation and amplification according to the manufacturer’s protocol ( CG000582 ). Autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed before imaging and decoding signals on the Xenium analyzer. The Xenium slide processing and Xenium analyzer loading were performed at Northwestern University NUSeq core facility.    scRNA-seq data analyses  All scRNA-seq datasets were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database or the European Molecular Biology Laboratory-European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) database. These databases include  GSE176063  and  GSE172127  (E14.5 mouse fetal liver),  GSE108097  (mouse bone marrow and spleen),  GSE134355  and  GSE120446  (human bone marrow) and E-MTAB- 7407  (human fetal liver). The datasets were analyzed using Giotto Suite (v.4.0.5) or Seurat (v.5.0.3) in R (v.4.3.3). For the Giotto Suite and Seurat analyses, the workflows were reported on the following websites:  https://giottosuite.com/articles/singlecell_prostate_standard.html  and  https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/pbmc3k_tutorial , respectively. In brief, the Giotto object was created after reading barcodes, features (genes) and matrix files. Then, the Giotto object was filtered, using expression threshold = 1, features detected in minimal cells = 50 and minimal detected features per cell = 500, followed by normalization with the scale factor = 6,000. The cells were removed when the percentage of the standard mitochondria gene was more than 15%. Feature and cell statistics were calculated. Dimension reduction was performed by calculating highly variable features and running a principal component analysis. The nearest neighbor network was created, and UMAP was run with the parameter dimensions to use = 1:10. The cells were clustered using a nearest neighbor network and the Leiden community detection algorithm with a resolution of 0.2 to 0.5. For the combination analysis of multiple samples, a harmony integration algorithm was used. Cell marker genes were found and extracted with the scran package. Cell type annotation was done by combining marker genes, web databases including the mouse cell atlas  https://bis.zju.edu.cn/MCA , the human cell landscape  https://db.cngb.org/HCL  and the original published reports. After cell type annotation, cell metadata were extracted for downstream pathway and differential gene expression analysis. Ligand and receptor information in the cell metadata was used to analyze the potential cell–cell interactions.    Visium spatial gene expression data analyses  For the Visium data, the original fastq datasets were analyzed using Space Ranger (10x Genomics;  https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/space-ranger/latest/tutorials/count-ffpe-tutorial ). The raw feature matrix and matched spatial image files were exported for further analysis with Giotto Suite (v.4.0.5) in R (v.4.3.3). The workflow for Visium transcriptomic data analysis has previously been reported  51  . In brief, the Giotto Visium object was created by reading barcodes, features (genes), matrix and image files, aligning the metadata and images, and transforming tissue barcodes into cell IDs. Then, the Giotto Visium object was filtered, using expression threshold = 1, features detected in minimal cells = 50 and minimal detected features per cell = 1,000, followed by normalization with the scale factor = 6,000. Similarly, feature and cell (spot) statistics were calculated. Dimension reduction was performed by calculating highly variable features and running a principal component analysis. Then,  t -distributed stochastic neighbor embedding and UMAP were run with the parameter dimensions to use = 1:10. A nearest neighbor network was created, and cells were clustered based on the nearest neighbor network and the Leiden community detection algorithm with a resolution of 0.2 to 0.5. Different clusters were mapped in situ to show their spatial distributions. Marker genes in each cluster were found and extracted with the scran package. Given that each spot contains the mixed transcriptome of several cells and each cluster is equivalent to a bulk RNA-seq dataset, cell type enrichment was performed using the PAGE method, in which 20 marker genes per cell type were derived from the cell metadata of the matched scRNA-seq dataset, and the relative expression scores (also called  z -scores) of each cell type were calculated.  Z -scores of all cell types were extracted, and correlations between every two kinds of cells were calculated. The spatial distributions of each cell type were mapped in situ.    Workflow of Xenium spatial gene expression  For Xenium data, the original fastq datasets were analyzed by Space Ranger (10x Genomics;  https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/space-ranger/latest/tutorials/count-ffpe-tutorial ). Cell feature matrix, cell boundary, nucleus boundary, transcript files and spatial morphology image files were exported for further analysis with Giotto Suite (v.4.0.5) in R (v.4.3.3). The workflow of the Xenium transcriptomic data analysis was previously reported  51  . In brief, the Giotto Xenium object was created after loading the probe, matrix and image files and then integrating the metadata, cell boundary and nucleus boundary images. Then, the Giotto Xenium object was filtered using expression threshold = 1, features detected in minimal cells = 3 and minimal detected features per cell = 5, followed by normalization with the scale factor = 5,000. Feature and cell statistics were calculated. Dimension reduction was performed by calculating highly variable features and running a principal component analysis. Then,  t -distributed stochastic neighbor embedding and UMAP were run with the parameter dimensions to use = 1:10. A nearest neighbor network was created, and cells were clustered based on the nearest neighbor network and the Leiden community detection algorithm with a resolution of 0.2 to 0.5. Different clusters were mapped in situ to show their spatial distributions. Marker genes in each cluster were found and extracted with the scran package. Finally, cell type annotation was performed by combining marker genes, web databases including the mouse cell atlas  https://bis.zju.edu.cn/MCA , human cell landscape  https://db.cngb.org/HCL  and cell metadata of the matched scRNA-seq dataset. The spatial distributions of each cell type were mapped in situ. The spatial Delaunay network was calculated with maximum distance = 400. Cell proximity enrichment with 1,000 simulations was performed to show potential cell–cell interactions.    Combined RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence staining  Combined RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence was performed as per the manufacturer’s instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific). FFPE blocks were sectioned under RNase-free conditions at the Mouse Histology and Phenotyping Laboratory, Northwestern University, then deparaffinized with HISTO-CLEAR II (National Diagnostics) and heat-pretreated. Following hydrophobic barrier application, samples underwent sequential protease digestion, fixation, probe hybridization, amplification and labeling using mouse C1qa (VB6-14028-VT) and Tyrobp (VB1-19392-VT) ViewRNA Tissue Probe Sets (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Slides were then blocked with Odyssey Blocking Buffer (LI-COR, 30 min, room temperature), incubated with primary antibody (anti-TER-119, 14-5921-82, Thermo Fisher Scientific) overnight at 4 °C, washed four times with 1× PBS/0.1% Tween-20 and incubated with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-rat IgG secondary antibody (1 h, room temperature). After DAPI counterstaining and mounting, images were acquired on a ZEISS microscope.    Bone marrow transplantation  C1qa-heterogeneous mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory and crossed to obtain C1qa knockout mice. Bone marrow transplantation was performed as previously reported  52 – 54  . In brief, total bone marrow cells from C1qa knockout and age-matched wild-type mice were collected, RBC-lysed and transplanted into lethally irradiated recipients. Then, 2 months post transplantation, peripheral blood was collected for complete blood count analysis, and bone marrow was collected for further study.    Co-culture of BMDMs and erythroblasts  Macrophages derived from mouse bone marrow were isolated and induced as described in a previous study  55  . In brief, wild-type mice were killed, and total bone marrow cells were isolated from their femurs. Then, the cells were cultured in DMEM/F-12 supplemented with 10% FBS (GeminiBio), 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 100 ng ml −1  macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF; StemCell Technologies) for 7 days. At the same time, lineage-negative cells from the bone marrow of wild-type mice were isolated and purified as described in previous studies  13 , 56 , 57  . Then, the lineage-negative cells were co-cultured with BMDMs in a six-well plate. For each well, 1.5 × 10 6  macrophages and 4.5 × 10 6  lineage-negative cells were co-cultured in 2 ml fresh Epo-containing medium for 48 h. Pure human C1qa protein was purchased from Abcam (cat. no. ab282858), and 25 µg ml −1  C1qa protein and vehicle solution were added at the beginning of co-culture. After co-culture, the cells were collected and analyzed by flow cytometry.    Cryosection of mouse femur without decalcification  The femur was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 72 h, then embedded in 8% gelatin (8 g of gelatin in PBS) and stored at −80 °C for 24 h before cryosectioning following a published report  25  . Cryosectioning was performed at −25 °C, with the femur sectioned into 100 µm-thick slices and collected onto coated microscope slides. These slides were equilibrated to room temperature. During equilibration, differences in the coefficients of expansion between the bone and bone marrow allowed easy separation of the bone from the marrow while preserving the structural integrity of the marrow. The bone marrow was then embedded in paraffin and sectioned onto spatial transcriptomic-dedicated slides for transcriptome analysis.    Culture of human iPS cells  Human iPS cell line SCTi003-A (cat. no. 200-0510) derived from peripheral blood mononuclear cells from a 48-year-old healthy female donor was purchased from StemCell Technologies. SCTi003-A is karyotypically stable, shows trilineage differentiation potential and expresses markers of the undifferentiated state following reprogramming using a non-integrating reprogramming technology. The iPS cells were maintained in mTeSR Plus medium (StemCell Technologies, 85857) in six-well plates coated with 10% (v/v) hESC-Qualified Matrix (Corning, CLS354277) diluted in DMEM/F-12 medium (Gibco, 10565018). The iPS cells were passaged using ReLeSR (StemCell Technologies, 100-0483) and routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination and karyotype for quality control.    Bone marrow organoid differentiation  The bone marrow differentiation protocol was derived from the method described previously  35 – 37  . Specifically, iPS cells were dissociated using ReLeSR when colonies reached approximately 100 μm in diameter during the differentiation phase. The iPS cell aggregates were incubated overnight in mTeSR Plus medium enhanced with RevitaCell in six-well Costar Ultra-Low Attachment plates (Corning, CLS356230; cat. no. 3471). Following this incubation, cells were gathered by gravitation in a 15 ml Falcon tube (Fisher Scientific, 11507411) and resuspended in Phase I medium. This medium consisted of APEL2 (StemCell Technologies, 05275) enriched with bone morphogenic protein 4 (BMP4; Thermo Fisher Scientific, PHC9531), fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2; StemCell Technologies, 78134.1) and vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGF-165; StemCell Technologies, 78159.1) at 50 ng ml −1 . The cells were then plated in six-well ultra-low attachment plates and incubated under hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 , 5% CO 2 ) for 3 days (days 0–3). After this period, cell aggregates were collected by gravitation and suspended in Phase II medium for an additional 48 h (days 3–5). The Phase II medium included APEL2 supplemented with BMP4, FGF2 and VEGFA at 50 ng ml −1 , along with human Stem Cell Factor (hSCF; StemCell Technologies, 78062) and Fms-like tyrosine kinase-3 Ligand (Flt3; StemCell Technologies, 78009) at 25 ng ml −1 . On day 5, cells were again collected by gravity for hydrogel embedding. The hydrogels, composed of 60% collagen (types I and IV mixed at a 1:1 ratio, purchased from Advanced Biomatrix, 5022 and 5007) and 40% Matrigel (Corning, CCLS356230), were prepared on ice according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Next, a 0.5 ml cell-free base layer was laid and allowed to polymerize for 2 h, followed by another 0.5 ml layer containing the cell aggregates, also left to polymerize for 2 h at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . The fully polymerized gels with cell aggregates were then supplemented with Phase III media. This media included VEGFA at 50 ng ml −1 , VEGFC, FGF2, BMP4, hSCF, Flt3, Epo (StemCell Technologies, 78007), thrombopoietin (StemCell Technologies, 78210) and granulocytic colony-stimulating factor (StemCell Technologies, 78012) at 25 ng ml −1 , along with IL-3 (StemCell Technologies, 78194) and IL-6 (StemCell Technologies, 78050) at 10 ng ml −1 . The media was refreshed every 72 h. On day 12, the organoids were released from the 3D culture matrix and transferred to 96-well ultra-low attachment plates (Thermo Fisher, 174929) in Phase IV medium (APEL2 with 2% FBS, supplemented with VEGFA, VEGFC, FGF2, hSCF and Flt3 at 25 ng ml −1 , and thrombopoietin, Epo, IL-3 and IL-6 at 10 ng ml −1 ). Phase IV medium was replaced every 72 h at a 50:50 ratio. The organoids are fully matured from day 21 and ready for experiments.    Bone marrow organoid immunostaining and imaging  Organoids were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (30 min, room temperature), permeabilized with 0.25% Triton X-100/PBS (1 h) and blocked with 5% goat serum/0.1% Tween-20/PBS (1 h, orbital shaker). Primary antibodies—anti-CD68 (Abcam, ab783; 1:200), anti-CD235a (Invitrogen, PA5-141179; 1:300) and biotin-UEA1 (Vector Lab, B0-1065-2; 1:300)—were applied overnight at 4 °C on an orbital shaker, followed by three washes with 0.1% Tween-20/PBS. Fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies and streptavidin were incubated overnight at 4 °C, washed three times, then once with PBS. Organoids were cleared in 60% glycerol/2.5 M fructose (1 h) and transferred to glass-bottom dishes for imaging.  Whole-mount confocal imaging was performed on a Nikon AXR system using a ×20 water-immersion objective (CFI Apo LWD Lambda S 20XC WI), capturing 100 µm in depth at 0.8 µm Z-steps. Z-stacks were 3D-reconstructed in Imaris 10.0 (Oxford Instruments). To quantify erythroblast–macrophage spatial associations, 90 randomly placed 15 µm-diameter spheres were generated per organoid, and nearest neighbor distances between erythroblasts, macrophages and random spheres were calculated across three independent organoids.    Flow cytometry analysis of human bone marrow organoids  Organoids were collected by sedimentation, washed twice with PBS and dissociated in 20 mg ml −1  collagenase type II (Sigma-Aldrich, C6885) in HEPES buffer (Sigma-Aldrich, H0887) by sequential 5-min incubation at 37 °C, trituration and 15 min incubation. Dissociated cells were resuspended in 5 ml PBS, filtered through a 40 µm strainer, centrifuged (300 g , 5 min) and resuspended in 100 µl PBS for immunostaining with APC-conjugated anti-CD235a (BioLegend, HI264) and FITC-conjugated anti-CD71 (BioLegend, CY1G4) for 15 min at room temperature. After washing, cells from ten pooled organoids per condition were analyzed by flow cytometry (BD FACSymphony A3) with single-color and fluorescence-minus-one controls.    Flow cytometry analysis of human bone marrow aspirate samples  Fresh human bone marrow aspirate samples were obtained from leftover diagnostic specimens at Northwestern Memorial Hospital under IRB approval (IRB ID STU00217116). Samples were diluted 1:20 in MACS buffer (PBS containing 2 mM EDTA and 0.5% BSA). A total of 100 µl of the diluted bone marrow was stained with the following antibodies: FITC-conjugated anti-CD71 (BioLegend, clone CY1G4), APC-conjugated anti-CD235a (BioLegend, clone HI264) and BV421-conjugated anti-ICAM4 (BD, clone 729632). Fluorescence-minus-one controls were prepared using BV421-conjugated mouse IgG2b, κ isotype control antibody (BD, clone 27-35), in combination with FITC-conjugated anti-CD71 and APC-conjugated anti-CD235a antibodies. For each sample, at least 5,000 CD71 + CD235a +  events were recorded using a BD FACSymphony A3 flow cytometer. MFI of ICAM4 expression was quantified using FlowJo (v.10.0).    Multiplexed immunofluorescence staining  FFPE sections were dewaxed and rehydrated at the Mouse Histology and Phenotyping Laboratory, Northwestern University. Antigen retrieval was performed in boiling 1× citric buffer (pH 6.0, Sigma-Aldrich) for 10 min. After cooling and three PBS washes, slides were blocked with Odyssey Blocking Buffer (LI-COR, 30 min, room temperature), incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, washed four times with PBS, then incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained with Hoechst 33342 (2 µg ml −1 ; Invitrogen, 15 min), washed, coverslipped and imaged on a ZEISS microscope. Primary antibodies included anti-TER-119 (14-5921-82, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and anti-C1QC/C1QG (BS-11337R, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Secondary antibodies were mouse anti-rat IgG2b (50-4815-82) and goat anti-rabbit IgG Alexa Fluor 488 (A11008), both from Thermo Fisher Scientific.    MethoCult Assay with antibody treatment  Human CD34 +  HSPCs (StemCell Technologies, 70008.1) were seeded at 1 × 10 3  per well in six-well plates using EPO-only MethoCult medium (StemCell Technologies, 04330) supplemented with IgG isotype control (Invitrogen, 02-6102), anti-ICAM4 (PA5-112917), anti-RHAG (PA5-51097) or anti-CD51 (MA5-32195) at 12.5 µg ml −1 . After 14 days at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 , plates were imaged using inverted wide-field microscopy (Evos M5000). Cells were collected by dissolving the MethoCult gel in MACs buffer (0.5% BSA, 2 mM EDTA in PBS) and centrifugation (500 g , 15 min), counted using an automated cell counter (TC20, Bio-Rad) and immunostained for flow cytometry analysis.    Statistics and reproducibility  For the comparison of two groups, Student’s  t -test or Welch’s  t -test (two-tailed) was used. For comparing more than two groups, a one-way ANOVA was used. For the correlation analysis of two groups of cells, Pearson correlation coefficients were computed, and 95% confidence intervals and two-tailed  P  values were determined. Individual data points are shown in all figures. Data distribution was assumed to be normal, but this was not formally tested. All statistical analyses were performed using R or GraphPad Prism 10.6. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. No data were excluded from the analyses. Sample assignment to experimental groups was based on genotype, age or disease status rather than randomization, as the study design involved predefined biological comparisons between distinct groups; no additional randomization was applied to data collection or experimental conditions. evidence_text: Iron-catalyzed oxidative stress reveals an exposome-related ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche in BRCA1-linked renal carcinogenesis. Early cancer initiation under chronic oxidative stress requires the survival of epithelial cells that should otherwise be eliminated by regulated cell death. However, the spatial and morphological identity of such stress-adapted cells remains poorly defined. Here, we integrated Xenium single-cell spatial transcriptomics, quantitative nuclear morphometrics, mitochondrial analyses, and human cancer datasets to investigate iron-driven renal carcinogenesis in Brca1(L63X/+) rats. Ferric nitrilotriacetate exposure induced dynamic remodeling of proximal tubular epithelium, characterized by loss of homeostatic transport and mitochondrial programs, and activation of Myc, Met, Lcn2, Anxa2 and iron-handling genes. BRCA1 haploinsufficiency expanded a karyomegalic proximal tubular state associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, chromatin hyperchromasia, nuclear remodeling, and ferroptosis-resistant transcriptional features. Subclassification of karyomegalic cells identified distinct stress-adaptive populations, including a BRCA1-associated K2 state enriched for Myc/Met/Lcn2 signaling and preferentially embedded within a pro-oncogenic epithelial-stromal microenvironment. Of note, neighboring non-karyomegalic proximal tubular cells acquired related iron-handling and survival-biased programs, indicating that karyomegaly marks a broader pre-neoplastic field rather than an isolated abnormality. Human TCGA renal cancer analyses and morphometric assessment of BRCA1-mutant breast tissue further supported the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated gene modules and nuclear remodeling. These findings define a spatially organized, ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche as an early lesion in iron-driven carcinogenesis and establish quantitative nuclear morphology as a functional readout of exposome-related oxidative stress adaptation in genetically susceptible tissues. mutant) rat     n.s.   not significant     NSD   nuclear substructure density     OA_PT    oxidative stress–adaptive  proximal tubule     OCR   oxygen-consumption rate     PCA   principal component analysis     PFI   progression-free interval     PII   peripheral intensity index     PT   proximal tubule (tubular cell[s])     RCA   rolling circle amplification     RCC   renal cell carcinoma     REF   rat embryonic fibroblast     ROI   region of interest     ssGSEA   single-sample gene set enrichment analysis     ST   stromal cell(s)     STN   solid tissue normal (non-tumorous portion)     TA   tissue array     TCGA   The Cancer Genome Atlas     TEM   transmission electron microscopy     TR_PT    transient regenerative  proximal tubule     UMAP   uniform manifold approximation and projection     WSI   whole slide image (imaging)     WT   wild-type       1  Introduction  Iron is essential for life [ 1 ], yet its redox activity also drives oxidative reactions that promote mutagenesis and malignant transformation [ 2 , 3 ]. Although persistent oxidative stress is increasingly recognized as a trigger of tumor initiation, how damaged epithelial cells survive this hostile redox environment and acquire tumor-initiating potential remains poorly understood. We previously established a ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA) model of Fenton reaction–driven carcinogenesis that reproducibly induces metastatic renal adenocarcinomas and enables mechanistic analysis of oxidative stress–mediated tumorigenesis [ [4] ,  [5] ,  [6] ]. However, the spatially organized molecular programs that allow a subset of injured epithelial cells to evade elimination and persist as pre-neoplastic precursors have not been defined.  Hereditary cancers account for 5–10% of human malignancies [ 7 , 8 ]. Among hereditary cancer genes,  BRCA1  and  BRCA2  are best known for their association with breast and ovarian cancers [ 9 ], but growing evidence suggests broader roles in epithelial cancer susceptibility, including renal cell carcinoma [ 10 , 11 ]. We recently established Brca1/2 haploinsufficient rat models that recapitulate key aspects of human disease [ [12] ,  [13] ,  [14] ]. Notably, Fe-NTA–induced carcinogenesis is markedly accelerated in Brca1 haploinsufficient rats and accompanied by recurrent  c-Myc  amplification and mitochondrial abnormalities during early tumorigenesis [ 15 , 16 ]. These findings raise the possibility that BRCA1 deficiency promotes the emergence of stress-adaptive epithelial states that evade ferroptotic elimination during tumor initiation.  Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics enable single-cell–resolution molecular profiling while preserving tissue architecture and histological context [ 17 ]. Here, we integrated Xenium-based spatial transcriptomics with quantitative digital nuclear morphometrics to investigate early carcinogenic processes under iron-driven oxidative stress. This approach identified a previously unrecognized ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic epithelial population associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, oncogenic signaling, and iron-handling programs. Integration with human cancer datasets further suggested that related stress-adaptive programs and nuclear abnormalities may be relevant to human epithelial tumorigenesis. Together, our findings establish a spatial and morphological framework for understanding how exposome-related [ 18 ] oxidative stress intersects with hereditary susceptibility during the earliest stages of tumor initiation.    2  Materials and methods   2.1  Renal carcinogenesis model by ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA)  All the animal experiments were approved by the animal experimental committee of Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine.  Sprague-Dawley  strain male rats of wild-type (WT) and  Brca1(L63X/+ ; mutant, MUT) [ 12 ] were bred as described previously [ 15 ]. Representative kidney specimens of 1 and 3 weeks under the carcinogenesis protocol were obtained and fixed either in phosphate-buffered 10% formalin for 48 h for paraffin-embedding, or 2 % glutaraldehyde in 1 mM phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for resin-embedding.    2.2  Tissue array construction  Six formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) rat kidney samples were organized into a tissue array (TA) format to enable simultaneous Xenium processing (three samples per slide; two slides per instrument run). RNA quality was pre-verified by RNAScope in situ on the sections from all the donor blocks. After confirmation, sample area was selected and manually extracted to re-form new TA blocks with samples coring within proper size of area (∼12 mm × 24 mm). From each TA block, 5 μm sections were cut with a rotary microtome (Leica RM2135) and mounted onto  Xenium  adhesive slides (10x Genomics). Sections were dried overnight, then stored in a desiccator until processing. All cutting and mounting steps were performed with precautions to maintain tissue morphology and RNA integrity (sterile, RNase-free tools and surfaces).    2.3  Gene panel design  A custom 50-gene  Xenium In Situ  probe panel (ID:  TCMFHM ) was designed for  Rattus norvegicus  using the 10x Genomics Custom Panel Designer ( Table S1 ). Target genes were selected to represent major renal cell types and key kidney injury pathways, prioritizing established marker genes for nephron segments (proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct principal/intercalated cells), glomerular cell types (podocytes, endothelial), interstitial cells (stromal cells), immune infiltrates (inflammatory cells), and urothelium, alongside transcripts implicated in our previous differential expression array analyses [ 15 , 19 , 20 ]. Gene selection was further guided by a published rat kidney single-cell transcriptomic atlas (E-GEAD-450 [ 21 ]), retaining only genes with robust, cell type-specific expression in the reference dataset. The final panel included renal biomarkers and ferroptosis-, oncogenic/tumor suppressor-, mitochondria-associated genes relevant to renal pathophysiology [ 15 , 22 ]. Probes were tiled across exonic regions with high specificity, minimizing off-target homology and maximizing RNA accessibility; negative control and decoding control probes were included for quality control [ 23 ].    2.4  Xenium in situ workflow  FFPE tissue sections (5 μm) were processed using the Xenium FFPE in situ transcriptomics protocol (10x Genomics, v1.0; Demonstrated Protocol  CG000580 ;  Fig. 1 A). Briefly, sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, subjected to antigen retrieval and RNA exposure, and enzymatically digested under RNase-free conditions to facilitate probe penetration while preserving tissue morphology. Probe hybridization was performed at 50 °C for approximately 18 h. After stringent washes, adjacently hybridized probe pairs were ligated for 2 h at 37 °C and amplified by rolling circle amplification (RCA) for 2 h at 30 °C to generate detectable signals [ 24 ]. Tissue autofluorescence was reduced by chemical quenching, and nuclei were counterstained with DAPI for visualization and segmentation. Processed slides were mounted in Xenium imaging buffer, sealed in Xenium cassettes, and stored at 4 °C in the dark until analysis.  Fig. 1   Xenium in situ enables spatially resolved single-cell atlas of the rat kidney with customized gene panel.  A,  Experimental workflow: Wild-type (WT) and  Brca1 -mutant (MUT) rats received ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA) treatment and were dissected at the indicated time-points (control, 1 week, 3 weeks) to obtain kidneys. Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) sections were processed on the Xenium platform. Following in-situ transcript capture and high-plex imaging, the identical sections were stained with H&E to provide histological context (Scale bars, 10 μm).  B , UMAP embedding of Xenium-profiled cells from the WT control kidney, marked by cell-type annotation derived from canonical marker genes ( Table S1 ).  C,  Dot-plot of the top markers per cell type. Circle size indicates the percentage of nuclei expressing the gene; color denotes mean of normalized expression (z-scored).  D,  WT control renal cortex: H&E image overlaid with Xenium-decoded cells colored by cell-type annotation in B (scale bar, 100 μm).                        2.4.1  Xenium analyzer instrument  Automated imaging and transcript decoding were performed on the 10x Genomics Xenium Analyzer using software v2.0.1.0. The instrument acquired high-resolution images through 15 iterative cycles of fluorescent probe binding, imaging, and signal removal. Four fluorescent channels were used per cycle, allowing each gene in the custom panel to be identified by a unique optical barcode. Images were acquired at 200 nm/pixel resolution with a 20× objective, and Z-stack images were collected at 0.75 μm intervals. Adjacent fields of view were tiled and computationally stitched using DAPI nuclear signals as fiducial landmarks to generate a registered whole-tissue image.  Transcripts were decoded by matching fluorescent puncta to the predefined barcode codebook. Only transcripts with a Q-score ≥20, corresponding to approximately 99% decoding accuracy, were retained for downstream analysis [ 23 ]. Detected transcripts were exported with XY coordinates, gene identities, and Q-scores. Negative-control probe signals accounted for <0.03% of total reads, indicating low background noise.    2.4.2  Cell segmentation and transcript assignment  Cell segmentation was performed using the Xenium onboard segmentation pipeline. DAPI images were used to identify nuclear boundaries, which were expanded isotropically by up to 15 μm or until they reached neighboring cell boundaries. This nuclear expansion method generated non-overlapping cell polygons approximating renal epithelial cell boundaries. Decoded transcripts located within each polygon were assigned to the corresponding cell, producing a cell-by-gene expression matrix for downstream single-cell spatial analysis [ 23 ].    2.4.3  Post-Xenium histology  After transcript profiling, the same tissue sections were re-stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) to correlate molecular data with tissue morphology. H&E images were acquired using a Leica Aperio AT2 slide scanner at 40× magnification and processed in QuPath 0.5.1 to generate OME-TIFF files. The H&E images were then aligned to DAPI images in Xenium Explorer, allowing transcript-defined cell types and spatial regions to be evaluated in relation to histological structures, such as glomeruli and renal tubules.     2.5  Bioinformatic analysis of spatial transcriptomics data   2.5.1  Data preprocessing and normalization  Xenium outputs (six rat kidney FFPE tissue samples: WT_CT, MUT_CT, WT_Fe1w, MUT_Fe1w, WT_Fe3w, MUT_Fe3w) were loaded into R (version 4.4.1) and converted to a Seurat object using Seurat v5.0.1. All data normalization was performed by SCTransform to stabilize variance transformation and to regress out sequencing-depth effects. This yielded log-normalized count data (stored in Seurat “SCT” assay) for each sample, mitigating technical variability while preserving biological variation. Low-quality cells (e.g. with extremely low transcript counts) were minimal due to Xenium's preprocessing and only cells with nCount_Xenium >0 were retained.    2.5.2  Data integration and clustering  Following normalization, the unified object containing data from six samples was processed for joint analysis. We re-ran SCTransform (merged), PCA (all genes; 30 PCs), FindNeighbors (dims 1–30), FindClusters (resolution 2.0), and UMAP (PCA), which yielded multiple clusters with distinct transcriptional signatures. Mixing across samples in PCA/UMAP was inspected to verify minimal batch effects. Clusters were manually annotated to kidney lineages (proximal tubule, stromal, endothelial, loop of Henle, collecting duct principal/intercalated, podocyte, inflammatory, proximal-like) based on canonical markers [ 21 ] and spatial context provided by Xenium Explorer. For focused analyses, we subset proximal_tubules and stromal_cells contents and re-ran the same pipeline on (i) the merged dataset to confirm lineage assignments and (ii) each compartment separately to resolve fine subclusters (pt_n; st_n) for downstream analyses.    2.5.3  Pathological score maps  Proximal-tubule clusters were defined into four pathology groups by expressional signatures and tubular morphology: normal_tubules (PT_1,2,5,6,10,11), acute_injured (PT_8), subacute_injured (PT_0,3,4,7), and dying_tubules (PT_9). Using Seurat v5.0.1 we set group identities and performed one-vs-rest DE per group with FindMarkers (two-sided Wilcoxon; min.pct = 0.2, logfc.threshold = 0.25, only.pos = TRUE). The top 10 genes by avg_log2FC per group were used for visualization (group-wise AverageExpression heatmap, z-scored by gene). For quantitative per-cell scores, we computed module scores with AddModuleScore on the available marker genes for each group (requiring ≥5 genes), using nbin = 3 and ctrl = 10 to ensure robust background control on the limited panel. Scores were then row-matched by cell_ID and merged into the Giotto (v4.2.0) object's cell_metadata for downstream spatial mapping. All plotting of score maps used fixed global min–max limits per score and unified diverging palettes to enable cross-sample comparison.    2.5.4  Morphological-transcriptomics analysis of nuclei  Nuclear polygons from Xenium segmentation (“nucleus_boundaries.csv.gz”) were imported into R (sf v1.0.19; tidyverse v2.0.0) to compute per-nucleus morphometrics: nuclear area, eccentricity (elongation, 0–1), circularity (4π·area/perimeter 2 ), compactness, convexity, solidity (area/convex hull area) and perimeter/area ratio (boundary irregularity). Polygons were linked to the same cell barcodes used in Seurat; analyses were restricted to proximal tubule cells with expression taken from the SCT assay.  For each gene–feature pair, we fit single-cell linear models per FOV (WT_Fe3w: FOV_3; MUT_Fe3w: FOV_6) with the morphology feature z-scored and technical covariates (library size, detected features) included; slopes (β) and two-sided  P  values were recorded and FDR-adjusted within FOV (Benjamini–Hochberg). As robustness checks, we computed Spearman correlations and ran elastic net models (glmnet) to assess whether multiple features jointly predict expression; a non-zero coefficient denoted feature selection.  To obtain genotype-robust effects, per-FOV slopes were combined by sample-size–weighted averaging (pooled β), and per-FOV  P  values were combined by Stouffer's method (weights ∝ √n), followed by FDR across all pairs. For each gene we derived a “consensus rank” integrating pooled β, pooled FDR, and elastic-net selection.  To identify coordinated programs, each gene was represented by its vector of pooled β across morphology features. Cosine similarity was computed between genes; pairs with similarity ≥0.6 were connected and clustered by Louvain community detection to define morphology-linked gene modules.    2.5.5  Quantification of nuclear phenotypes and integration with transcriptomics  For fields of view (FOVs) from WT_Fe3w (FOV3) and MUT_Fe3w (FOV6), nuclei were segmented using Cellpose (v2.3.2; pretrained nuclei model) [ 37 ]. Three per-cell nuclear morphological readouts were derived from the hematoxylin channel (skimage.color.rgb2hed) within each nuclear mask: (i) hematoxylin optical density (HOD), mean channel intensity following Gaussian smoothing (σ = 0.5 μm); (ii) nuclear substructure density (NSD), the count of intranuclear hematoxylin-dense foci, detected after within-nucleus 2nd-98th percentile normalization, Otsu thresholding, and filtration by area (0.3–6.0 μm 2 ) and circularity (4πA/P 2  ≥ 0.40), expressed per 100 μm 2  of nuclear area; and (iii) peripheral intensity index (PII), (mean        H  O  D   periphery      − mean        H  O  D   interior     )/section-median HOD, where peripheral (distance ≤ s) and interior (distance > s) zones were defined from a Euclidean distance transform of the nuclear boundary at shell thicknesses  s  ∈ (0.5, 1.0, 1.5) μm ( Fig. S4C ); section-median HOD was estimated once per FOV from a random sample of ∼2000 nuclei.  Cellpose-segmented nuclei were assigned Xenium cell identity via two-stage spatial registration. First, an existing QuPath-to-Xenium cell correspondence (established by manual landmark selection and iterative refinement) provided position anchors for an affine transform between the FOV image and Xenium coordinate spaces. Second, true nuclear centroids (QuPath nucleus geometry) were matched to the affine-registered Cellpose nuclei by reciprocal nearest-neighbor matching within the shared coordinate space, at the tightest tolerance (0.5–5 μm ladder) retaining ≥90% of the maximum achievable match count. PT filtering was performed after registration to avoid selection bias. Registration accuracy was confirmed by comparing QuPath's measurements (HOD;  Fig. S4A ) against Cellpose/scikit-image values.    2.5.6  Gene–morphometry association models (HOD/NSD/PII)  For each gene     g     and within a condition (WT_Fe3w; MUT_Fe3w) independently, a single-cell ordinary least-squares model was fitted:     Y  i   =  α  +   β  g   ·   X   i  g    +  γ   A  i   +   ϵ  i     where      Y  i      is the nuclear morphometric readout for cell     i     (HOD; NSD;       P  I  I   s     ),      X   i  g       is the log 1 p-normalized Xenium transcript count for gene     g     in cell     i    , and      A  i      is Cellpose-measured nuclear area (μm 2 ). Two-sided Wald p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons across 50 genes within each condition (Benjamini–Hochberg, FDR <0.05). Cross-condition concordance was assessed by Pearson correlation and sign agreement of per-gene      β  ˆ      between FOVs. Estimates were pooled by fixed-effects inverse-variance weighting:      β  ˆ    F  E    =     ∑  k    w  k     β  ˆ   k      ∑  k    w  k     ,   w  k   =  S   E  k   −  2      with pooled Wald z-statistics BH-FDR corrected across all 50 genes. Models were implemented in Python (statsmodels v0.14; scipy).    2.5.7  Karyomegaly sub-stratification and peri-karyomegaly analysis  PT cells from merged Xenium dataset were defined as karyomegalic (enlarged) if nuclear area > mean+2SD within the PT cell population, and elongated if major/minor axis ratio >2. SCTransform-normalized RNA counts from karyomegalic cells were stored as a SCTx assay. Morphological features processed from nuclear polygons were stored as a MORPH assay and reduced by PCA.  Karyomegalic PTs were then reclustered by a weighted nearest-neighbor (WNN) model that integrates RNA and morphology: SCTx PCA (dims 1–30) and a PCA of z-scored morphology (dims 1–6) were combined with FindMultiModalNeighbors (modality weights recorded as SCTx.weight/MORPH.weight), followed by UMAP on the weighted graph and Louvain communities on wsnn; we grid-searched morphology PCs (2-4, 6) × resolution (0.2, 0.3) and selected the setting with the highest mean silhouette in the WNN UMAP, followed by further resolution tuning, yielding the final result (K0–K5, resolution 0.15). Gene markers were computed using Seurat FindAllMarkers (logistic regression with covariates sample, fov_num, nCount_SCTx). Morphology tiles report per-feature means with significance from two-sided linear models (BH-FDR <0.05).  Spatial context was obtained by overlaying subcluster labels onto H&E in Xenium Explorer (Fe-NTA, 3-week). For peri-karyomegalic analyses, each karyomegalic PT served as a center; PT neighbors within 30 μm were compared with PTs >30 μm away, and hallmark expression visualized as z-scored heatmaps/dot plots (Wilcoxon, BH-FDR where indicated).    2.5.8  Neighborhood composition and microenvironment analysis  Cell centroids (centroid_x, centroid_y) and annotations from the Seurat metadata were filtered to proximal_tubules and stromal_cells, and used for point map plotting and neighbor-associated computations. Independently for each sample, the number of stromal neighbors within a 30 μm Euclidean radius was recorded for each PT cell, by a KD-tree constructed over stromal cell centroids (FNN v1.1.4.1, R; k ≤ 500). Group differences were assessed by Kruskal–Wallis test; pairwise post-hoc comparisons used Dunn's test with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction (rstatix v0.7.3, R). Beyond cell-intrinsic analysis, we modeled proximal-tubule/stromal spatial organization with Giotto (v4.2.0; Python backend) [ 25 ]. For each field, we constructed a radius-based neighbor graph (30 μm) to capture tubulointerstitial contacts in renal tissue [ 26 ]. Community detection on this neighborhood graph using the Leiden algorithm (findNetworkCommunities) yielded microenvironment (ME) clusters, i.e., spatially coherent neighborhoods that may contain mixed PT (pt_n) and stromal (st_n) subtypes. We quantified the cell-type composition and contact enrichment for each ME cluster (normalized by cell abundance). ME prevalences were compared across the six samples to assess genotype/treatment effects. ME labels were overlaid on tissue images in Xenium Explorer to verify anatomic plausibility.  To test whether ME states were independent of karyomegalic clusters, we constructed a WNN-karyomegalic × ME contingency table and applied a Pearson χ 2  test of independence (chisq.test) Tiles in the heatmap display standardized Pearson residuals (Haberman adjustment, chis$stdres): positive (green) indicates over-representation; negative (red) indicates under-representation. Significance stars denote: ∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  1.96    , ∗∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  2.58    , and ∗∗∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  3.00    . Global association was summarized by Cramér's     V  =     χ  2   /   (   N   [   min  ⁡   (   r  ,  c   )   −  1   ]    )       ; extremely small P values are reported as thresholds (e.g.,     p  <  2.2  ×   10   −  16      ).    2.5.9  Data visualization  All data visualization was performed in R (v4.4.1), using ggplot2 and plotters bundled with Seurat unless noted otherwise. Low-dimensional embeddings (UMAP) were rendered with DimPlot and annotated by cluster, sample, or FOV; single-gene summaries used VlnPlot or Seurat DotPlot. Heatmaps were produced with ComplexHeatmap for clustered expression/annotation panels and pheatmap for compact correlation/residual matrices. Panel assembly used patchwork/cowplot with harmonized color palettes, fixed aspect ratios for spatial panels, and consistent legends/scales. Multi-panel gene maps ( Fig. 2 C) and pathology-score maps ( Fig. 3 E) were generated in Giotto and exported in R. Xenium Explorer was used only to overlay labels on H&E/DAPI micrographs. Differential expression (DE) used Seurat FindMarkers/FindAllMarkers on SCT-normalized data with two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Genes were eligible if detected in ≥5% of cells in either group; we report avg_log2FC (positive = higher in the first group), pct_in/pct_out, and adjusted P. Multiple testing was controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg; genes with FDR <0.05 and log 2 FC ≥ 0.25 were considered significant. Random subsampling (set.seed 42) was applied only to downsample points for visualization and was never applied in statistical testing. Box-and-violin plots display median and inter-quartile range; error bars represent 95% confidence intervals unless specified. Because the Xenium dataset included one representative specimen per genotype/treatment condition, cell-level statistics were interpreted as discovery-level measures of spatial association or enrichment rather than animal-level biological replication; key conclusions were supported by prior Fe-NTA data, mitochondrial TEM/REF analyses, and TCGA-based human validation.    2.5.11  Code availability No new algorithms were developed for this manuscript. All code created for analysis is available from the authors upon request.  Mitochondrial cristae morphometry analysis  Transmission electron microscopic images were acquired on a JEM-1400PLUS (JEOL; Tokyo, Japan). Images were analyzed in Fiji/ImageJ (v1.54p). After pixel calibration, individual mitochondria were manually outlined as ROIs with area (μm 2 ) recorded. Within each ROI, cristae ridges were segmented using Trainable Weka Segmentation (Fiji) to obtain a probability map for cristae vs. matrix. High-confidence pixels were thresholded and processed with Ridge Detection to obtain ridge centerlines, followed by Skeletonize (2D/3D) and Analyze Skeleton to quantify branch geometry. Derived per-mitochondrion metrics were: Total cristae length (μm) = Σ branch lengths;  Mean branch length (μm) = Σ branch lengths / number of branches;  Cristae length density (μm/μm 2 ) = total cristae length / mitochondrial area.   Metrics were exported as CVS files and plotted in R.    2.7  Immunoblotting  Kidney cortex lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer, resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred by standard methods. Primary antibodies included: anti-FTMT (ab124889, Abcam), anti-Mfrn1 (PA5-26720, Invitrogen), anti-Mfrn2 (PA5-42498, Invitrogen); anti-ACTB (AC-15, Sigma) served as loading control. Bands were quantified in ImageJ, normalized to ACTB, and analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (unpaired  t -test; significance thresholds: ∗ P  < 0.05, ∗∗ P  < 0.01, ∗∗∗ P  < 0.001; n.s., not significant).    2.8  Primary rat embryonic fibroblasts (REFs) and treatments  REFs were derived from E13–15 embryos by standard protocols [ 28 ]. Genotypes and sex were determined by PCR [ 15 , 29 ]. Male-derived WT and Brca1-MUT REFs were maintained in DMEM (043-30085, Wako, Osaka, Japan) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Biowest; Nuaillé, France) and Mito + Serum Extender (355006, Corning, USA). REFs were immortalized via lentiviral transduction of SV40 (Addgene#22298) packaged with pspAX2 (#12260) and VSV-G (#14888). For oxidative stress, cells were treated with Fe-NTA (500 μM, 6 h) prior to fixation.    2.9  Immunofluorescence (confocal)  Cells were fixed, permeabilized and stained with anti-TOM20 (11802-1-AP, Proteintech) and anti-γ-H2AX (05-636, Sigma-Aldrich); nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. A Zeiss confocal microscope (LSM880, Carl Zeiss) was applied for image acquisition.    2.10  Mitochondrial respiration  Oxygen consumption (OCR) and extracellular acidification (ECAR) were measured on a Seahorse XFe24 Analyzer (Agilent) following manufacture's instructions. Briefly, REFs were seeded (6 × 10 4 /well) in Seahorse XF DMEM (103575-100) supplemented with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine (103577/8/9-100) on a Seahorse XFe24 plate and incubated overnight. The XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (103015-100) was run with sequential injections of oligomycin 1.5 μM, FCCP 1 μM, and rotenone/antimycin A 0.5 μM. Cell count was quantified using BioTek Cytation 5 and Keyence BZ-X800 for normalization. Data were processed per manufacturer's instructions and analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (unpaired  t -test with significance shown in  Fig. 8 E ).    2.11  TCGA transcriptomic cohorts  To evaluate the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated transcriptional programs identified in our experimental model, we analyzed data obtained from the TCGA Pan-Cancer Clinical Data Resource, for TCGA-KIRC as the primary validation cohort, and additional tumor types for exploratory analyses, including TCGA-BRCA, TCGA-COAD, TCGA-LIHC, TCGA-LUAD, and TCGA-LUSC [ 30 ].  RNA-seq data were retrieved via TCGAbiolinks v2.32.0 [ 31 ] from the NCI GDC. Tumor-adjacent solid tissue normal (STN) samples were used for the primary analyses, whereas primary tumor samples were evaluated separately for independent validation. Raw counts were normalized by the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method using edgeR v4.2.2 [ 32 ] and converted to log 2 -counts per million (log 2 -CPM; prior count = 1). For duplicate gene entries, the isoform with the highest mean expression was retained.   2.11.1  Karyomegalic module definition and scoring  Four gene modules were evaluated (Fig. S7A). Three gene modules were defined based on findings from our Xenium spatial transcriptomics data. Module activity was quantified by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) using GSVA v1.52.3 [ 33 ], computed independently within each tissue compartment (STN or tumor). Only modules with at least three genes present in the expression matrix were retained. Patient-level scores were derived as mean across available samples.    2.11.2  Survival analysis  Clinical annotations, including progression-free interval (PFI) and overall survival (OS), were obtained from curated TCGA clinical datasets. For each module, patients were stratified into high- and low-score groups using the cohort-specific median module score as the cutoff. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated using the survival and survminer packages.  Associations between module activity and clinical outcome were evaluated using log-rank tests and univariable Cox proportional hazards models. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated from Cox models. Analyses were performed separately for PFI and OS endpoints. Cohorts with fewer than five outcome events or insufficient matched samples were excluded from survival testing.  A tiered strategy was used for Multiple-testing correction. We designated TCGA-KIRC as the confirmatory cohort and analyzed non-renal cancer cohorts in an exploratory manner. Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was therefore performed separately within confirmatory and exploratory tiers. Statistical significance was assessed primarily using the tier-specific FDR-adjusted results.    2.11.3  BRCA1 mutation carrier and control definition  BRCA1 germline carriers were defined as described [ 34 ]. Non-carrier controls were identified by a two-tiered exclusion strategy requiring availability of diagnostic WSIs and absence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, RAD51C, RAD51D, BARD1, and NBN. Controls were further selected by two-stage propensity score matching to control for clinical covariates [ 35 ] .  The final cohort comprised 20 BRCA1 germline carriers and 63 matched non-carrier controls (76.2% ductal, 4.8% lobular, 19.0% other histological subtypes).    2.11.4  Histopathological image analysis  Diagnostic whole slide images (WSIs) for TCGA-BRCA were obtained from the NCI Genomic Data Commons (GDC). Germline variant data were accessed from the TCGA PanCanAtlas Germline dataset [ 34 ] under controlled GDC access (dbGaP: phs000178), in compliance with the TCGA data use agreement.  Regions of interest (ROIs) containing well-formed ductal tubules were manually annotated in ductal carcinoma WSIs from both groups using QuPath v0.4 [ 36 ] (15 controls, 7 carriers; ROI count was limited by preserved adjacent normal portions). Nucleus segmentation was performed using Cellpose v2.3.2 [ 37 ], and morphological features were extracted using scikit-image. A post-hoc quality filter was applied to remove spurious detections. Nucleus-level analyses are presented as exploratory findings; patient-level analyses constitute the primary statistical inference.      3  Results   3.1  Xenium in situ on early stages of Fe-NTA-induced renal carcinogenesis  To identify early alterations during iron-driven renal carcinogenesis, we analyzed kidneys from wild-type (WT) and  Brca1  mutant ( L63X/+ ; MUT) rats subjected to Fe-NTA administration, as previously described [ 15 ]. Because rat-compatible spatial transcriptomic panels remain limited, we designed a custom 50-gene Xenium panel covering renal structural markers from single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets [ 21 ], together with genes related to iron metabolism, mitochondrial function, and tumorigenesis based on our previous studies [ 5 , 38 ].  Six kidney samples representing control, 1-week, and 3-week Fe-NTA exposure in WT and MUT rats were analyzed across two Xenium slides. DAPI-based segmentation captured approximately 324,765–531,476 cells per sample, with median transcript detection of 62–104 transcripts per cell ( Fig. 1 A). Post-Xenium H&E staining preserved tissue morphology and enabled direct integration of spatial transcriptomics with histopathology ( Fig. 1 A–D). Seurat-based clustering identified 53 cellular clusters, which were annotated into 10 major renal cell categories based on marker expression and histological context ( Fig. 1 B and C;  Fig. S1A and B ). Molecular annotations closely matched H&E-defined structures, supporting robust cell-type assignment even with a focused gene panel ( Fig. 1 D). Cluster composition varied across genotype and treatment conditions, with prominent changes in proximal tubules and stromal cells ( Fig. S1C ), indicating early remodeling of epithelial and interstitial compartments during Fe-NTA-induced carcinogenesis.    3.2  Characterization of key-gene signatures in early renal carcinogenesis  We next focused on transcriptional remodeling of proximal tubular cells (PTs), the principal target of Fe-NTA-induced renal carcinogenesis. Refined clustering of PT and stromal compartments improved resolution of treatment- and genotype-associated cell states ( Fig. S2A and B ). Single-cell expression analysis revealed reciprocal regulation of homeostatic and injury-associated genes in PTs ( Fig. 2 A). In control kidneys, PTs highly expressed renal function and mitochondrial metabolism genes, hereafter referred to as “friend key-genes,” including  Lrp2, Pink1,  and  Amacr . In contrast, Fe-NTA exposure induced “foe key-genes” associated with injury and tumorigenesis, including  Myc, Met, Lcn2 , and  Anxa2 , with concomitant reduction of homeostatic markers.  Several foe key-genes were induced as early as 1 week after Fe-NTA exposure in both genotypes ( Fig. 2 A). Although  Met, Anxa2, Lcn2, Sfxn3 , and  Klf4  showed partial reduction by 3 weeks,  Myc  and  Slc22a17  remained elevated or further increased. At 3 weeks, MUT PTs showed stronger expression of foe markers than WT, whereas  Lrp2  and  Amacr  were more strongly reduced, indicating genotype-dependent epithelial remodeling under oxidative stress. Spatial mapping with Giotto confirmed that friend key-genes were enriched in intact tubular segments, whereas foe key-genes localized to histologically abnormal regions with tubular dilation, disruption, or loss of recognizable tubular organization ( Fig. 2 C).  Because karyomegalic PTs are a characteristic lesion in Fe-NTA-treated kidneys [ 39 , 40 ], we quantified nuclear morphology using Xenium-derived nuclear polygons ( Fig. 2 B). Fe-NTA exposure was associated with nuclear enlargement, reduced compactness and circularity, and increased eccentricity. WT karyomegalic cells had larger nuclei than MUT cells under comparable treatment conditions ( Fig. S5A ). These data indicate that nuclear remodeling accompanies early Fe-NTA-induced epithelial injury and is modified by Brca1 haploinsufficiency.    3.3  Dynamics of diverse PT subtypes in early renal carcinogenesis  To resolve PT dynamics during early carcinogenesis, we reclustered PTs and identified 11 subtypes ( Fig. 3 A and B). Homeostatic PT clusters 1, 2, 5, 6, 10, and 12 predominated in control kidneys and expressed renal functional and mitochondrial genes. In contrast, clusters 0, 3, 4, 7, 8, and 9 emerged after Fe-NTA exposure and showed increased injury-, repair-, or foe key-gene expression with reduced homeostatic programs. Genotype-specific differences became evident after Fe-NTA exposure: WT kidneys showed transient loss of normal tubular states at 1 week with partial recovery by 3 weeks, whereas MUT kidneys showed expansion of injured clusters, particularly clusters 4 and 7.  The PT subtypes represented distinct biological states ( Fig. 3 B). Oxidative Stress–Adaptive PTs (cluster 0; OA_PT) expressed antioxidant and metabolic genes such as  Cubn, Slc40a1, Lrp2, Slc27a2 , and  Gpx4 , together with moderate  Myc  and  Met  expression. DNA Damage–Response PTs (cluster 3; DR_PT) expressed repair and regenerative markers including  Mki67, Rad51, Bard1 , and  Bap1 . Maladaptive Repair PTs (clusters 4 and 7; MR_PT) expressed  Lcn2, Slc22a17 , and other foe key-genes, with cluster 4 retaining more friend key-gene expression than cluster 7. Transient Regenerative PTs (cluster 8; TR_PT) expressed proliferation and DNA repair markers, whereas Ferroptotic PTs (cluster 9; Fer_PT) were often isolated necrotic or pyknotic cells within otherwise preserved tubules, as confirmed by Xenium Explorer alignment with H&E images ( Fig. S3A ).  Spatially, DR_PT localized mainly near the cortex–medulla boundary in WT kidneys at 1 week but was less evident in MUT kidneys ( Fig. 3 C). MR_PT populations frequently co-localized within MUT tubules, whereas WT tubules showed greater admixture of homeostatic, oxidative stress–adaptive, and transient regenerative states. Stromal reclustering further identified 13 stromal subtypes with genotype- and treatment-dependent composition ( Fig. 3 D). After 3 weeks of Fe-NTA, MUT kidneys showed expansion of stromal states enriched for regenerative, injury-response, iron-handling, matrix-remodeling, and macrophage-recruiting signatures, including ST_1, ST_3, ST_5/8, ST_6, and ST_9.  To summarize PT status spatially, we generated pathology-informed module scores ( Fig. S3B–D ). Spatial score maps showed that normal tubular scores declined after 1 week of Fe-NTA exposure and partially recovered in WT kidneys by 3 weeks, whereas MUT kidneys showed more persistent dysfunction ( Fig. 3 E). Interestingly, scores representing renal injury and cell death (acute/subacute injured score; dying tubules score) displayed inverse spatial patterns to normal tubules score at 1-week Fe-NTA treatment, with reduced acute injured score at 3-week Fe-NTA treatment, marking the progression of homeostatic PT clusters toward subacute injury and the initiation of cellular adaptations linked to ferroptosis resistance and potential oncogenic transformation.    3.4  Nuclear morphometrics reflect transcriptional behaviors in pathological/genotype-dependent patterns  We next asked whether nuclear morphology captures transcriptional states at single-cell resolution. Morphological features derived from Xenium polygons included nuclear area, eccentricity, circularity, compactness, convexity, and solidity ( Fig. 4 A). Gene–morphology associations were quantified using covariate-adjusted linear models with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction. In Fe-NTA 3-week samples, morphology-associated coefficients revealed coordinated relationships between nuclear shape and PT transcriptional state ( Fig. 4 B). Oncogenic and iron-associated genes, including  Lcn2, Anxa2, Met, Pcbp2, Myc , and  Sfxn3,  were positively associated with eccentricity and convexity, whereas circular and compact nuclei were associated with preserved PT markers such as S lc27a2, Lrp2, Pink1,  and  Tfrc . Although the overall direction of associations was similar between WT and MUT kidneys, MUT showed stronger coefficients, indicating amplified coupling between nuclear morphology and stress-associated transcription under Brca1 haploinsufficiency.  We then converted morphology–gene β profiles into gene–gene networks using cosine similarity. Under the pre-specified criteria of FDR ≤0.05, β ≥ 0.10, and cosine ≥0.70, robust modules were absent in control kidneys and WT Fe-NTA 3-week kidneys, whereas WT Fe-NTA 1-week kidneys showed compact Slc27a2–Lrp2–Pink1 and Mki67–Anxa2 modules ( Fig. 4 C). In contrast, MUT kidneys retained modules at both 1 and 3 weeks, including a recurrent Slc27a2–Lrp2 core and an Lcn2–Anxa2 injury-associated core, suggesting genotype-dependent persistence of morphology-linked transcriptional programs.  To identify transcriptional correlates of nuclear chromatin organization during early carcinogenic nuclear transformation, we derived three nuclear morphometric parameters: hematoxylin optical density (HOD), nuclear substructure density (NSD) [ 41 ], and peripheral intensity index (PII) [ 42 ], from H&E images of WT and MUT Fe-NTA 3w kidneys. HOD provided quantitative readout of bulk nuclear chromatin compaction. In WT, the genes most strongly associated with HOD (e.g.,  Gpx4 ,  Fth1 ,  Ncoa4 ,  Pcbp1 , Tfrc) were uniformly negative, indicating that more robust iron-homeostatic programs correspond to lower nuclear hematoxylin density, consistent with a more open chromatin state ( Fig. 4 D;  Table S2 ). In MUT, PT identity genes (e.g.,  Amacr ,  Slc27a2 ,  Lrp2 ) again showed strong negative associations, whereas top positive associations were observed for  Sfxn3 ,  Sting1 ,  Mcub ,  S100a9 ,  Anxa2 , and  Lcn2 , suggesting that chromatin compaction is associated with mitochondrial alteration and stress responses in Brca1 deficient carcinogenesis. Despite that majority of significant genes were genotype-specific, effect direction was replicated across genotypes for  Lrp2 ,  Slc27a2 , and  Amacr  (negative in both) and for  Lgals1 ,  Anxa2 ,  Pcbp2 , and  Bard1  (positive in both). Fixed-effects meta-analysis was consistent with an overall pattern during oxidative stress-based carcinogenesis, where homeostatic genes downregulate with chromatin compaction, while carcinogenetic pathways across injury/iron-overload/fibrosis are activated, especially more pronounced in  BRCA1  mutants.  NSD [ 41 ], which detected hematoxylin-dense intranuclear foci, showed no detectable gene-level association in either genotype ( Fig. S4B ), consistent with its proposed role as constitutive, transcriptionally silent chromatin compartment (e.g., chromocenters). PII captured the distribution of peripheral heterochromatin (lamina-associated domains (LADs)), providing a complementary readout of nuclear architectural organization. In WT, PT metabolic genes (e.g.,  Pink1 ,  Slc27a2 ,  Tfrc ,  Fth1 ,  Gpx4 ,  Ncoa4 ,  Pcbp2 ) were positively associated with PII, indicating that they correspond to greater peripheral enrichment of condensed chromatin, consistent with intact LAD organization ( Fig. 4 E;  Table S2 ). In MUT,  Slc27a2 ,  Amacr , and  Lrp2  retained similar positive associations, while  Mcub ,  Sting1 , and  Cdkn1/2a  showed significant negative associations not observed in WT, implying a distinct transcriptional signature related to peripheral heterochromatin loss [ 43 , 44 ]. As with HOD, cross concordance was low overall, although  Slc27a2 ,  Gpx4 , and  Pink1  replicated a consistent positive direction in both genotypes. Meta-analysis identified positive pooled effects for PT/iron/mitochondrial metabolic genes (e.g.,  Lrp2 ,  Slc27a2 ,  Amacr ), alongside negative effects including  Cdkn1/2a ,  Mcub ,  Lcn2 ,  Myc , and  Lgals1  ( Fig. 4 E).  Together, these results indicate that HOD and PII both capture a shared transcriptional axis linking proximal tubule homeostasis to chromatin reorganization, with this signature more extensive in MUT. These findings also demonstrate that nuclear chromatin morphometry can be systematically linked to spatial transcriptomic profiles, identifying candidate chromatin-state markers of early renal carcinogenesis.    3.5  Epithelial karyomegaly classified into subtypes with distinct biological signatures  We defined karyomegalic epithelial cells as PTs with nuclear area greater than mean + 2SD and elongated cells as those with axis ratio >2. Compared with other PTs, enlarged nuclei showed consistent  Cdkn1a  upregulation and  Pink1  downregulation, with heterogeneous induction of DNA damage repair and regenerative genes ( Fig. 5 A;  Fig. S5C and D ). Elongated cells showed impaired epithelial function with increased  Sfxn3  and modest  Rad51  and  Mki67  induction ( Fig. S5B ). Because karyomegalic cells showed clear transcriptional heterogeneity and group-dependent differences in incidence, we focused subsequent analyses on enlarged epithelial nuclei. We next investigated the morphological and transcriptional features of re-clustered karyomegalic subpopulations. Among all clusters, K1 displayed the most pronounced nuclear enlargement with irregular, rough nuclear contours, and thus most closely aligned with the canonical pathological definition of karyomegaly ( Fig. 5 B, D). Transcriptional profiling further revealed strong induction of  Cdkn1a , coordinated with elevated  Ncoa4  and reduced  Fth1 , indicative of stress-associated cell-cycle arrest with an active ferritinophagy-mediated iron-mobilization program ( Fig. 5 C, S5E). K4 was enriched for markers of proximal tubule homeostasis and metabolic competence (e.g.,  Lrp2, Slc27a2, Amacr, Pink1 ), suggesting maintenance of epithelial transport and mitochondrial quality control in WT ( Fig. 5 B, C). And in morphological perspectives, K4 showed relatively more solid and compact nucleus. Strikingly, K2 and K5 co-expressed  Met, Lcn2,  and  Myc , pointing to an adaptive stress program with oncogenic features, whereas significant nuclear morphology features included elongation yet smaller area than K1. We interpret these states as a potential early pro-tumorigenic niche in BRCA1-haploinsufficient kidneys that may represent an actionable window for intervention in carcinogenesis.  To determine whether karyomegaly represents not only an altered epithelial state but also a local epithelial microenvironment, we profiled PT neighbors located within 30 μm of either karyomegalic or non-karyomegalic PT cells. PTs adjacent to karyomegalic cells showed increased expression of iron-handling, oxidative stress–adaptive, and pro-survival genes, including  Lcn2, Anxa2, Mki67, Sfxn3, Cdkn1a,  and  Myc , together with reduced  Amacr, Aqp3,  and  Pink1  ( Fig. 5 E). These signatures partially mirrored those of karyomegalic cells themselves, indicating that surrounding epithelial cells acquire a stress-adapted, survival-biased state. This interpretation is supported by the induction of factors linked to ferroptotic vulnerability, including  Lcn2 , which can modulate labile iron availability and antioxidant defenses [ 45 ], and by reduced  Pink1 , suggesting impaired mitophagy [ 46 ].  Subtype-stratified analysis further showed that PTs surrounding K2 cells were enriched for  Myc, Lcn2, Slc40a1,  and  Met , with reduced  Amacr, Pink1,  and  Slc27a2,  whereas PTs surrounding K4 cells maintained metabolic and mitochondrial homeostasis genes ( Fig. 5 E). Thus, karyomegalic states appear to act as focal organizers of local epithelial programs, with BRCA1-haploinsufficient karyomegaly defining a stress-adaptive, iron-handling, proto-oncogenic niche permissive for iron-driven carcinogenesis.    3.6  Stromal neighbors contribute to distinct regulatory system in BRCA1-MUT kidneys  Because renal epithelial injury occurs within an integrated tubulointerstitial environment [ 47 , 48 ], we examined stromal proximity and microenvironmental organization.
