To characterize these changes, we performed Leiden-based microenvironmental (ME) clustering, using previously defined PT and stromal subclusters within a 30 μm radius. Twelve predominant MEs were retained for analysis ( Fig. 6 B;  Fig. S6B ). ME_2 and ME_5 showed marked differences between WT and MUT kidneys after 3 weeks of Fe-NTA exposure ( Fig. 6 C). Spatial projection revealed that ME_2 localized mainly to the cortex–medulla boundary, whereas ME_5 predominated in the upper cortex ( Fig. 6 D). ME_2 was enriched in WT_Fe3w and contained stromal programs associated with cell cycling, DNA repair, and moderate injury responses. In contrast, ME_5 predominated in MUT_Fe3w and showed stromal signatures related to iron storage, ferroptosis protection, matrix remodeling, and angiogenesis, including  Fth1, Ftl1, Pink1, Ncoa4, Gpx4, Slc40a1, Vegfa,  and  Col3a1  (Figs.  3D  and  6 B;  Fig. S6C ). Oncogenic genes such as  Anxa2  and  Lcn2  also showed distinct interaction patterns between the two MEs, suggesting different epithelial–stromal regulatory states under oxidative stress. To assess mitochondrial function, we established immortalized primary rat embryonic fibroblasts (REFs) from male WT and Brca1-MUT embryos ( Fig. 8 C). After Fe-NTA-induced DNA double-strand breaks, MUT REFs showed fragmented mitochondrial networks, whereas WT cells retained more fused or branched mitochondria ( Fig. 8 D). Three modules were derived from karyomegalic clusters in the rat model: KaryoCore ( CDKN1A, MET, LCN2, SLC11A2 ), representing shared karyomegalic identity; Karyo2 ( COL3A1, MYC, SFXN3, SLC22A17, VEGFA, BRCA2, LGALS1, CGAS, MCUB ), representing the BRCA1-associated oncogenic K2 state; and Karyo4 ( AMACR, PINK1, UMOD, LRP2, SLC27A2 ), representing a homeostatic karyomegalic state. A literature-curated FerroResistance module ( GPX4, SLC7A11, AIFM2, NFE2L2, HMOX1, NQO1, FTL, GSS ) [ [49] ,  [50] ,  [51] ] was also evaluated ( Fig. S7A ).  In TCGA-KIRC tumor-adjacent solid-tissue-normal samples (STN; n = 72), higher KaryoCore and Karyo2 activity was associated with shorter progression-free interval (PFI) and overall survival (OS), whereas Karyo4 and FerroResistance were not significant in this compartment ( Fig. 9 A). In TCGA-KIRC primary tumors (n = 537), Karyo4 was associated with favorable OS and PFI, whereas Karyo2 was associated with adverse outcomes for both endpoints. FerroResistance showed a concordant adverse association with PFI, while KaryoCore was not prognostic in tumors. These associations were not reproduced in other carcinoma STN cohorts examined (COAD, LUAD, LUSC), although LIHC showed a non-significant adverse trend for Karyo2 ( Fig. S7B ). These results support Karyo2 and KaryoCore as renal pre-tumoral risk signals rather than generic pan-cancer markers. In  BRCA1 -mutant carriers, Karyo2 activity positively correlated with nuclear eccentricity (Spearman ρ = 0.82, p = 0.034), whereas KaryoCore activity correlated with nuclear solidity (ρ = 0.86, p = 0.024) ( Fig. 9 C). This stress-adaptive state was markedly expanded in Brca1 haploinsufficient rats, linking hereditary cancer susceptibility to impaired ferroptotic elimination under iron-catalyzed oxidative stress during tumor initiation. ( Fig. 7 ).  Spatial transcriptomics has transformed tissue biology by enabling molecular profiling while preserving histological architecture. Here, we further integrated spatial transcriptomic data with quantitative nuclear morphology derived from H&E sections. In diagnostic pathology, nuclear atypia remains one of the most fundamental indicators of cellular state, yet its quantitative integration with molecular programs has remained limited. By establishing digital metrics for nuclear size, contour smoothness, chromatin density, and nuclear substructure, we generated a framework that translates classical histopathological features into spatially resolved functional genomic states. This approach revealed that nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia closely track ferroptosis-resistant and stress-adaptive transcriptional programs during early carcinogenesis.  Our analysis identified a karyomegalic proximal tubular population enriched for oncogenic, iron-handling, and ferroptosis-resistance pathways. Importantly, neighboring non-karyomegalic epithelial cells displayed highly similar transcriptional profiles, suggesting that karyomegaly marks a broader pre-neoplastic field rather than an isolated cellular phenotype. Although karyomegalic cells themselves may represent a transient stress-adaptive state, they function as a histological beacon for the earliest detectable stages of tumor initiation under oxidative stress.  A central feature of this state was mitochondrial dysfunction. Electron microscopy previously demonstrated abundant small, interconnected mitochondria in  Brca1  mutant kidneys after Fe-NTA exposure [ 15 ], consistent with stress-induced mitochondrial remodeling. Concordantly, mitochondrial stress assays demonstrated impaired respiration and reduced metabolic flexibility, likely driven by a broad failure of mitochondrial quality control. Because mitochondria are major execution sites of ferroptosis [ 52 ], these alterations likely promote ferroptosis resistance and aberrant epithelial survival under iron-catalyzed oxidative stress. Reduced 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (HNE) production detected by HNEJ-1 staining may similarly reflect depletion of mitochondrial substrates for lipid peroxidation [ 15 , 53 ]. Further investigation into biogenesis and maintenance of the diminished functional mitochondrial pool will likely clarify how exposome-related iron stress establishes and sustains the ferroptosis-resistant niches. Moreover, Brca1 haploinsufficiency perturbs iron homeostasis even under physiological conditions [ 15 ], potentially increasing susceptibility to stress-adaptive transformation through heightened iron demand during DNA synthesis [ 54 ].  Importantly, integration with human cancer datasets suggested that this ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic state is conserved across multiple epithelial cancers beyond the experimental rat model ( Fig. 9 ). These findings support a broader model in which oxidative stress and hereditary susceptibility cooperate to generate stress-adaptive epithelial states that evade ferroptotic elimination during early tumorigenesis.  In conclusion, this study establishes a spatial and morphological framework for dissecting early tumor initiation by integrating single-cell spatial transcriptomics with digital pathology. We identify a ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic epithelial state associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and expanded under BRCA1 haploinsufficiency, linking nuclear morphology to stress-adaptive pre-neoplastic programs across experimental and human tissue contexts. These findings provide a framework for understanding how exposome-driven oxidative stress intersects with hereditary cancer susceptibility during the earliest stages of tumor initiation. Limitations include the use of a preclinical male rat model, a restricted Xenium gene panel, and representative rather than biologically replicated specimens for each Xenium condition. Accordingly, single-cell statistical significance should be interpreted as supporting spatial cell-state associations rather than animal-level biological replication, with biological relevance strengthened by independent mitochondrial analyses, prior Fe-NTA observations, and human TCGA validation. Future studies should determine whether targeting mitochondrial adaptation or ferroptosis resistance can prevent tumor initiation in genetically susceptible tissues exposed to carcinogenic oxidative stress. evidence_text:
GxP-Ready Single-Cell RNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics End-to-End Pipeline for Clinical Research. Single-cell/nucleus RNA-sequencing and Spatial Transcriptomics are powerful tools for investigating cellular heterogeneity and tissue architecture that have deepened our disease understanding. Their broader adoption in clinical and regulated settings, however, is hindered by regulatory requirements related to data integrity, regulatory compliance, reproducibility, and scalability. To address this gap, we developed NNclinSSOAP (Novo Nordisk Clinical Single-cell Spatial Omics Analytical Pipeline)-a modular, GxP-ready end-to-end computational pipeline that combines established single-cell workflows with a new Nextflow pipeline for Spatial Transcriptomics. NNclinSSOAP transforms RNA sequencing and Xenium spatial data into integrated, annotated single-cell objects and spatially resolved tissue maps. Designed to support mechanistic studies and clinical endpoint generation, it enables traceable and reproducible processing of large-scale datasets, scalable for use in HPC environments. Here, we provide a step-by-step demo case for using NNclinSSOAP that can be executed within 1.5 h on a standard laptop. All code and data are available open-source. Introduction  Single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) has revolutionized biological research by enabling the study of gene expression at the resolution of individual cells and nuclei. The technology allows for the identification of cell types, the characterization of cellular heterogeneity within tissues, underlying cell–cell communication, and the understanding of complex biological processes at an unprecedented level of detail [ 1 ]. This granularity can uncover rare cell populations, specific gene expression profiles, and dynamic changes over time [ 2 ]. However, it inherently lacks spatial [ 3 ] information, which is critical for understanding the tissue architecture and the local microenvironment in which the cells reside [ 4 ]. Conversely, Spatial Transcriptomics retains high-resolution spatial information but often lacks the single-cell resolution necessary to discern the complexity of cellular interactions and the interplay of different cell types within tissues [ 5 ].  The multimodal omics approach of combining scRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics addresses their respective limitations and provides a more comprehensive overview of cellular mechanisms in tissue contexts. This enables cellular identity and spatial organization to be established concurrently, which can aid in revealing the mechanisms of action of drugs and understanding disease pathology [ 6 – 8 ].  The use of these technologies and the large data handling requirements that come with them pose challenges for use in clinical settings. Ideally, such data need to be stored and handled in a Good Experimental Practice (GxP)-compliant way and compute resources need to be large enough to handle the data volumes.  This paper addresses these critical challenges, describing the implementation and usage instructions for NNclinSSOAP (Novo Nordisk Clinical Single-cell Spatial Omics Analytical Pipeline)—a GxP-ready pipeline for running sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics together. Our approach ensures data integrity and facilitates the translation of findings into robust and reliable conclusions for downstream applications, contributing to the standardization and quality control necessary for wider application of sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics in regulated environments and clinical trial settings. Unlike applications aimed primarily at interactive exploration, NNclinSSOAP is designed as an open-source, configurable pipeline that users can adapt to their own study designs, analysis needs, and compute environments.    Pipeline Overview  The development of this paper was motivated by the need for a combined sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics workflow in a clinical research and trial endpoint analysis context. While single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics technologies have become widely used for tissue and disease understanding for hypothesis generation, their application in regulated environments such as clinical trials presents specific challenges related to GxP requirements. Existing workflows, although effective in research settings, often do not address these requirements in a systematic way.  To meet these needs, we designed an end-to-end pipeline that integrates established methods and best practices from the broader community, with adaptations that ensure GxP-readiness and scalability. It was developed to ingest, process, and analyze sc/snRNA-seq and spatial data to generate clinical endpoints and run predefined analysis as per trial analysis plans, while providing a transparent and auditable framework suitable for clinical studies. Because of the number of samples set to be collected from multiple omics modalities, it was clear that the workflow would need to handle large data volumes and support execution in a high-performance computing (HPC) environment. To address these points, we adopted a modular, containerized architecture, enabling compliant storage and processing environments to be connected to the NNclinSSOAP pipeline.  The development process was iterative and collaborative, involving and building on cross-departmental expertise in computational biology, cloud engineering, statistics, and regulatory science. To address diverse data types and evolving analytical requirements, NNclinSSOAP was designed in a modular fashion that allows for straightforward adaptation to new datasets, data modalities, and requirements, providing flexibility and scalability for future research requirements and analyses. It is composed of 3 main components, connected as illustrated in Fig.  1  and described below:    1.  sc/snRNA-seq workflow: Handles the preprocessing, alignment, and quantification of single-nucleus RNA-seq data, leveraging nf-core/scrnaseq [ 9 ] for standardized and scalable data processing.    2.  R library/scripts: Enables advanced postprocessing, quality control, annotation, and statistical analyses of the output from the sc/snRNA-seq pipelines, ensuring robust downstream interpretation.    3.  SpatialXenium: A new Nextflow pipeline developed by us, designed to analyze multimodal data from the Spatial Transcriptomics platform Xenium [ 10 ], and optimized to run on HPCs ensuring efficient handling of large datasets. It ingests spatially resolved gene expression data and performs quality control, normalization, clustering, and spatial niche construction. The pipeline outputs processed Seurat objects (RDS), cluster/niche compositions, top marker genes, and visualizations (Principal Component Analysis [PCA], Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection [UMAP], and spatial plots). Optionally, it performs label transfer, adding cell-type annotation to the visualizations. The submodules that make up SpatialXenium are described in further detail in Box  1 .      Fig. 1.   Overview of how the 3 main components of NNclinSSOAP are connected, with their respective inputs, processing steps, outputs, and compute environments. (A) sc/snRNA-seq workflow. Processes fastq data, outputting, among others, h5ad files together with a multi-qc report and a BCO. The main processing steps include Quality control, Generate reference index, and Generate count matrix. (B) R library/scripts workflow. Processes the h5ad file from (A), outputting an annotated Seurat RDS object. The main processing steps include Quality control, Doublet detection, Multiple sample integration, Seurat object generation, Differential expression analysis, and Cell-type annotation. (C) SpatialXenium workflow. Processes raw Xenium data, outputting Spatial Transcriptomics analyses together with a report and a BCO, optionally taking the RDS object from the previous step to add cell-type labels to the analyses. The main processing steps include Quality control, Data normalization, Dimensionality reduction and clustering, Cell label transfer, and Results visualization.                     Box 1.   Brief introduction to the Spatial Transcriptomics processing steps (submodules)     1.

This further allows users to build and run NNclinSSOAP in cloud-based containers.  In practice, the “Methods” section in this paper outlines a demo case that enables users to familiarize themselves with NNclinSSOAP and convert raw sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics data into spatially resolved tissue maps with gene expression and cell-type annotations, through a small number of configuration changes and straightforward execution commands. The steps are divided into 2 procedures (Procedures 1 and 2) for sn/scRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics, respectively. These support local execution on the demo datasets and outline the possibility of deployment on cloud infrastructure for larger datasets. GxP-readiness  In this manuscript, GxP-readiness refers to the ability of a computational workflow to be deployed within a regulated clinical-research environment in a way that supports data integrity, traceability, reproducibility, auditability, and controlled change management. The term does not imply that the pipeline alone makes an analysis fully GxP compliant. Rather, NNclinSSOAP provides pipeline-level controls that can be combined with an institution’s validated infrastructure, standard operating procedures, access controls, and documentation practices. Relevant expectations for clinical computerized systems and analysis planning include principles described in ICH E6(R3) [ 11 ], ICH E9 [ 12 ], and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 [ 13 ].  NNclinSSOAP implements these pipeline-level controls through a modular architecture, containerized execution environments, and automatic provenance capture. The whirl package provides the functionality of executing scripts in batch and simultaneously getting a log from the individual execution [ 14 ]. Nextflow, an open-source workflow management system [ 15 ], allows each workflow step to be run as a specified module with captured parameters and process metadata, while containers help control software versions and dependencies. The entire workflow is documented automatically in BioCompute Objects (BCOs). They document the intended purpose, inputs, software and version identity, parameter settings, execution details, provenance, and output locations of an analysis, providing a standardized record that can be reviewed, repeated, and archived [ 16 , 17 ]. BioCompute is an FDA-supported standard for regulatory submissions, and can be used during regulated activities and communication with the agency [ 18 ].  In clinical use, the GxP-ready pipeline is intended to be executed after the analysis has been specified in the clinical study analysis plan. Input data, configuration files, and output objects are treated as controlled analysis artifacts. Sample metadata and QC thresholds are defined before execution where possible, the run is executed in a validated or otherwise qualified compute environment, and generated reports, logs, BCOs, and Seurat objects are retained as evidence of what was run.  In our implementation, clinical data storage and access are handled by a compliant Amazon Web Services (AWS) storage service with separate input and output locations and role-based access. For data processing, analyses were performed within a dedicated, GxP-validated compute environment developed in-house as part of the Novo Nordisk secure analytics platform. This environment operates within a cloud-based infrastructure to provide both scalability and regulatory compliance throughout the data life cycle. The flow of inputs and outputs and the environments used is shown in Fig.  1 . Other institutions can reuse the open-source code, containers, and provenance mechanisms that NNclinSSOAP provides, connecting the workflow to their own validated compute, storage, access-control, retention, audit-trail, and electronic-signature processes.  The scope of readiness is therefore layered. Elements that transfer directly with the pipeline include modular workflow definitions, container manifests, configurable analysis parameters, BCO generation, execution logs, and standard outputs for review. Elements that remain institution-specific include formal software validation or verification, training, role-based review and approval of BCOs, controlled versioning and change management of the validated pipeline, secure data retention, audit trails, and any electronic-signature practices. This distinction is important because BioCompute primarily defines what is documented. It does not replace local validation, governance, or standard operating procedures required for full GxP compliance.  Within the pipeline, GxP-readiness is also reflected in how analysis decisions are exposed rather than hidden. QC filters and label-transfer probability thresholds are explicit user-configurable parameters. Cells failing QC are excluded from downstream analysis according to documented thresholds, and low-probability labels are not silently converted into confident cell types. Instead, they are flagged as “Ambiguous” in the labeled Seurat metadata and visualizations and are accompanied by prediction files. This allows downstream users and reviewers to distinguish confident annotations from those requiring caution or manual review.    Applications  NNclinSSOAP was specifically developed for clinical trials incorporating transcriptomics as study endpoints, including sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Xenium. As a pioneering framework in the pharmaceutical industry, particularly for cardiometabolic diseases, NNclinSSOAP has already been used in 2 mechanism-of-action trials. The first trial, focused on Alzheimer’s disease, incorporated scRNA-seq data as a primary endpoint [ 19 ], and therefore utilized only Procedure 1, which is tailored for single-cell transcriptomics. In contrast, the second trial, a clinical study in kidney disease [ 20 , 21 ], employed both Procedures 1 and 2 as it included both snRNA-seq and Xenium Spatial Transcriptomics data.  By enabling rapid and GxP-aligned data processing, this workflow sets a new standard for transcriptomic analysis in clinical trials. Looking ahead, it is broadly applicable to trials in other therapeutic areas, provided that compatible input data are available. Thanks to Nextflow’s modular architecture, the workflow can be easily adapted to accommodate additional analytical modules in the future.  Notably, the SpatialXenium Nextflow pipeline described in this paper is publicly available as part of the repository and can be integrated into new or existing Nextflow workflows, independently of the broader workflow described in the paper.    Comparison to other methods  There are numerous tools and packages available to facilitate sc/snRNA Transcriptomics data preprocessing [ 22 ]. For sc/snRNA-seq, we used the established nf-core pipeline scrnaseq as part of Procedure 1. Beyond the initial preprocessing steps, downstream processing and analysis of sc/snRNA-seq data commonly leverage widely used packages such as Seurat [ 23 ] that we use as part of our R library. Our SpatialXenium pipeline is wrapped around the Seurat suite relevant for Spatial Transcriptomics data QC, preprocessing, and analytics.  Integrated platforms for combining single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics exist [ 24 ], but not as workflows aligned with GxP requirements. The purpose of this section is to contextualize NNclinSSOAP rather than to provide a formal benchmarking study. NNclinSSOAP builds on established community methods and combines them into a documented, containerized, and provenance-aware workflow for regulated clinical research settings. The points below therefore focus on workflow structure, traceability, reproducibility, and deployment considerations. Six main features make NNclinSSOAP different to other methods:    1.  Modularity. NNclinSSOAP not only makes it possible to run the underlying sc/snRNA-seq and SpatialXenium workflows separately, but the workflows themselves build on Nextflow modules. This simplifies both using the workflows and adapting them to future needs as well as making them scalable, a key factor in data heavy settings.    2.  GxP-readiness. Using Nextflow for building our workflows enables NNclinSSOAP to be both scalable and reproducible. Combined with BCO-based provenance capture, this supports selected GxP-relevant expectations, particularly traceability, reproducibility, and reviewability. It allows users to connect to a compute environment of choice, without compromising reproducibility, enabling analysis of data volumes at a much greater scale than in the demo case described in this paper. Full GxP compliance ultimately depends on deployment within an appropriate governed environment.    3.  The SpatialXenium pipeline. There is a publicly available pipeline, nf-core/spatialxe, currently under development. It is a flexible image- and coordinate-based reanalysis framework, focused on controlling and improving Xenium data quality through multiple segmentation and spatial-data methods. SpatialXenium differs from this, instead focusing on postprocessing and analysis of Xenium data. It provides users a fully specified, protocol-locked, and easily reproducible end-to-end pipeline, implementing Spatial Transcriptomics analysis from Seurat for Xenium data.    4.  We provide an R library capable of processing outputs generated by nf-core/scrnaseq, supporting standard Seurat workflows and downstream annotation. These scripts offer flexibility, incorporating tools such as Harmony [ 25 ] and RPCA [ 26 ] for multisample integration. For cell-type annotation, automated approaches like Azimuth [ 27 ] or SingleR [ 28 ] are supported, and user-defined reference datasets can be added. For differential treatment effect analysis, we use a pseudobulk [ 29 ] approach by aggregating counts per sample and cell type, followed by statistical assessment using edgeR [ 30 ], which enables robust testing of group-level differences while accounting for biological variability. Alternatively, other statistical methods can be integrated as needed. An overview of this workflow is illustrated in Fig.  1 .    5.  By leveraging the whirl package [ 14 ] to execute the R library, the pipeline produces a BCO along with multiple log files—one corresponding to each R script. The package offers the flexibility to modify certain domains within the BCO and to select specific scripts to run as needed.    6.  The R environment required for running these procedures is provided as a Docker container, ensuring that all necessary packages and dependencies are included and eliminating compatibility issues for the user. This approach allows the entire environment to be reliably loaded and the workflow to be executed as intended. However, one limitation is that package versions within the container may become outdated as new releases are made. Users also have the flexibility to set up and use their own custom environments if preferred.       Experimental Design   Expertise needed for implementation and interpretation  NNclinSSOAP was developed to be used by computational biologists, producing results (e.g., tables and figures) that can be interpreted and understood by medical or biological experts without a data science background. For users following the procedures step-by-step, no expertise is needed and none of the topics below need to be considered. However, some familiarity with single-cell transcriptomics and relevant training in statistical analysis of high-dimensional omics data and running analytics scripts is advisable for a smooth experience and ability to understand the outputs scientifically.  If the workflow outlined in this paper is adapted to another dataset different from the demo, carefully consider the points below. It is also recommended to read the extensive information and instructions provided in the code repository  README.md  and .md files in  /docs . For this, a broad understanding of R, Nextflow, cloud computing, containerization, and single-cell transcriptomics is needed.    Sampling strategy-dependent analysis  The datasets used in Procedure 2 contain a single sample each, one with healthy kidney tissue and the other with cancerous kidney tissue. This case facilitates analysis from the perspective of seeing differences in cell types and gene expression. Depending on a dataset’s sampling strategy, experimental design, and analysis plans, as often preregistered in a clinical trial setting, other relevant analyses and visualizations are possible, e.g., mitochondrial genes, cell cycle genes, biological sex-related genes, batch effect contribution from metadata, etc. For samples taken from the same subject at multiple time points (longitudinal data), it is possible to analyze changes over time. For samples taken at a single time point for multiple subjects (cross-sectional data), it is possible to analyze the homo-/heterogeneity within a population. Combining these 2 strategies creates a clinical trial scenario where NNclinSSOAP can be used to analyze subjects’ tissue characteristics over time as a response to treatment, comparing to a placebo group or among groups at a single time point for disease understanding.    Optional settings and configurations  Beyond the default settings and basic configurations required to run the demo case in the “Methods” section, NNclinSSOAP can be customized through various command line flags and configuration files. Figure  2  provides a high-level overview of these options.  For the sc/snRNA-seq workflow, users can customize the metadata and configuration files to use with their own data, according to the nf-core/scrnaseq documentation:  https://nf-co.re/scrnaseq/4.0.0/docs/usage/ . For improved version control and streamlined collaboration, it is highly recommended to maintain a dedicated Git repository containing all related metadata and configuration files.  Once the nf-core/scrnaseq pipeline has completed, NNclinSSOAP provides users with tools to further analyze and explore their data. Specifically, 3 main R scripts are included for downstream analysis (see Fig.  3 ), each designed with flexibility in both parameters and methods. To customize or modify the pipeline execution, users can edit the associated config file  preprocessing_workflow.yml . These options provide users with extensive flexibility for preprocessing, integrating, and annotating single-cell data within the NNclinSSOAP framework. Note that the RPCA integration method is computationally intensive and may not be suitable for local execution.    Fig. 3.   Summary of sc/snRNA-seq data analysis workflow and results. To load their own data into the pipeline, users must modify the  configs/read_samples.txt  file, ensuring it accurately lists each sample along with its corresponding metadata. Column names as well as visit and treatment arm values can be set from  configs/preprocessing_workflow.yml . All columns are intended to populate the Seurat object’s metadata, but if your dataset lacks certain variables (arm and visit), populate them with an NA and scripts 1 ( preprocessing_workflow.R ) and 2 ( cell_annotation.R ) will still function, allowing you to generate an integrated and annotated Seurat object.  Script 3 ( de_analysis.R ), designed for differential gene expression analysis in clinical settings to assess treatment response, specifically calculates treatment effects, which assumes the data are longitudinal, with 2 time points (a baseline and follow-up visit) and 2 distinct treatment arms (e.g., drug A and placebo), as is the case in the demo data (see Fig.  3 ). If your data are not longitudinal, this script can be excluded.  Since the pipeline is run using the whirl wrapper, users can also adjust the  whirl/_whirl_preprocessing.yml  and  whirl/_whirl_analysis.yml  config files to edit BCO domains or exclude scripts, such as  de_analysis.R , from execution as needed.  For SpatialXenium, the genes shown in the UMAP and spatial feature plots are read from  assets/genes.txt  in the Spatial Transcriptomics workflow. By default, this file contains the genes needed to reproduce our results on the demo case data. Users should adapt this file if using other datasets, to reflect their genes of interest. Multiple command line options control which cells and genes are included in the UMAP and spatial feature plots, and how strict the filtering is.    Quality control  QC thresholds should be reviewed in the context of each dataset and, where applicable, defined before downstream biological or clinical interpretation. For Xenium data, the relationship between read counts, gene detection, and QV score provides a practical check of assay quality (see Fig.  4 ). A high-quality dataset is expected to retain most informative cells and genes after filtering, with low-quality or control-probe-rich observations limited to a minority of the data. In contrast, a problematic dataset may show a large fraction of observations with low read counts, low QV scores, unusually high read-count outliers, or high control-probe proportions. The selected thresholds are captured in configuration files and execution outputs (see Fig.  2 ), supporting reproducibility and review of the filtering decisions.    Fig. 4. Seurat Spatial Transcriptomics visualization options  The tissue visualizations overlaid with gene expression and cell types generated from running SpatialXenium utilize the Seurat v5 package’s functions  ImageDimPlot() and  ImageFeaturePlot() . These offer a wide range of options beyond what is covered by default in SpatialXenium, enabling extensive control over plot aesthetics and content, including color scales, transparency, cell border properties, molecule overlays, coexpression blending for pairs of genes and grouping cell types. For advanced users wanting to tailor SpatialXenium visualizations to their specific biological questions,  ImageDimPlot()  is called from  label_transfers.r  and  ImageFeaturePlot()  is called from  plot_features.r . We strongly recommend familiarity with R, Seurat, and Nextflow for doing this, as making changes may result in errors downstream.  A vignette outlining the visualization possibilities can be accessed here:  https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/seurat5_spatial_vignette_2.html     Open-source strategy  Given the variability between clinical study designs and datasets, we chose to make NNclinSSOAP open-source, allowing users to adapt the pipeline beyond what is possible through the config and flag settings. This also allows users to use specific modules, such as SpatialXenium, instead of the entire pipeline. From a development and maintenance point of view, the open-source strategy invites users to contribute to the project as well as report any issues they encounter. Expected Results  The result of following both procedures is a transformation of raw sc/snRNA-seq data into an integrated and annotated Seurat object, and raw Xenium data into a spatially resolved cell object and map. This can aid in answering clinical questions, giving the user a deeper understanding of the analyzed tissues both at a cellular expression and a structural level, as is the case in the demo case data in this paper, highlighting differences between healthy and cancer kidney tissue.  When the procedures are executed with the supplied demo data using the specified software versions, parameters and settings, deterministic tables and files are expected to be reproducible. Stochastic visualization steps such as UMAP may show minor layout differences while preserving the same biological topology and interpretation. If the paper is followed using a personal dataset, the same types of outputs are expected, but results will differ according to the input data.   Sc/snRNA-seq (procedure 1)  Executing the sc/snRNA-seq workflow (Procedure 1, step 2) generates an nf-core results folder. The demo case dataset has been run with the cellranger aligner [ 31 ], so the results are the standard cellranger outputs. The special addition is the BCO object that has been generated since the plugin is included when running the nextflow pipeline.  In the second part of the workflow (Procedure 1, steps 4 and 5), each script produces a variety of plots and output files, which are organized into dedicated folders—see Box  2  for a summary of the results file structure.    •  Quality Control (QC): QC plots document the standard Seurat workflow, starting from reading the counts matrix and progressing through to the creation of the final Seurat object (see Fig.  3 A to D). A separate folder is generated for each sample’s QC outputs, while the integrated Seurat object is stored in the parent directory.    •  Cell Annotation: This step generates visualizations such as UMAPs displaying annotated clusters and violin plot displaying the annotation scores, along with an updated Seurat object that contains cell type assignments (see Fig.  3 E and F).    •  Differential Expression analysis: For each cell type, the pipeline outputs a normalized counts CSV file, a CSV file with differential expression results, and a volcano and line plot summarizing key findings (see Fig.  3 G and H). By using Nextflow, reports covering errors, timing and resource usage have automatically been created. An example results file structure is shown in Box  3 . To aid with technical and clinical interpretation, key outputs from Quality Control (QC), gene expression and cell type analysis are described in further detail below:    •  Quality Control: The QC plots (see Fig.  4 A and B) summarize how many genes and reads are captured per cell and how these values are distributed across the dataset. This allows users to identify low-quality cells, technical outliers, or regions with suboptimal capture efficiency before drawing any biological or clinical conclusion, ensuring that downstream patterns (e.g. “immune poor” areas) are not artifacts of poor data quality.    •  Gene Expression: The gene expression visualizations (see Fig.  4 C and D) show how the selected markers from  assets/genes.txt  are distributed both in UMAP space and across the tissue. Clinically, these plots help confirm that canonical markers (for example, tumor, immune, or stromal genes) are expressed in the expected tissue compartments and spatial niches, supporting interpretations such as tumor–stroma interactions, immune infiltration patterns, or localization of specific disease-relevant pathways.    •  Cell Type: The cell-type plots (see Fig.  4 E and F) resulting from the label transfer display the predicted cell types in UMAP space projected back onto the tissue, with cells below the chosen probability threshold set to “Ambiguous”. This makes it clear which assignments are robust enough to support biological or clinical interpretation, which should be treated with caution. In a clinical context, these maps can be used to explore how specific cell types (e.g., cytotoxic T cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells) are spatially organized within lesions, margins, or normal tissue, and how this architecture might relate to disease severity or therapeutic response.      Box 3.   Example file structure. Full sample file structure only shown for sample 1 for simplicity.   
     
      Conclusion  NNclinSSOAP offers a GxP-ready framework for scalable processing and analysis of single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics data for clinical research and trials. Its modular design and automated provenance capture ensure transparent, reproducible, auditable, and fully traceable analyses suitable for regulated environments, e.g., clinical trials. Together, these features provide a practical, unique, and extensible foundation for deploying multimodal transcriptomics across mechanistic studies and clinical trials. evidence_text:
DeSpaST: deconvoluting spatial transcriptomics signals to cell-level resolution using histology images. Advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies enable spatially resolved gene expression profiling, yet most platforms remain limited to spot-level resolution, where each measurement aggregates signals from multiple cells and obscures cell-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Existing computational approaches either provide limited sub-spot refinement or rely on matched single-cell RNA sequencing references that are costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we present DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network that deconvolves spot-level ST data into cell-level gene expression profiles using only paired histology images. DeSpaST extracts nucleus-level morphological features, constructs directed cellular interaction graphs, and integrates spatial and transcriptional information through message passing. Validated across four cancer datasets with orthogonal Xenium, immunofluorescence, ablation, and interslice evaluations, DeSpaST enhances spatial resolution, facilitates downstream cellular-level analyses, and provides deeper insights into tissue biology. Background  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have made significant progress in transitioning transcriptomic research from the cell level to a 2D spatial cell system. This transition is crucial for investigating cell–cell communication, tissue heterogeneity, and the tumor microenvironment, offering new insights into intricate biological processes. In contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), which requires tissue dissociation, ST technologies profile gene expression and preserve the spatial composition of cells within the native tissue environment [ 1 ]. ST technologies (e.g. 10× Genomics Visium [ 2 ], Nanostring GeoMx DSP [ 3 ], HDST [ 4 ], and Slide-seq [ 5 ]) utilize unique spatial barcodes to label the spatial locations and capture the gene expression at thousands of barcoded spatial locations (referred to as spots) within one experiment [ 6 ]. While these methods achieve high detection efficiency, their spatial resolution is inherently limited. The barcoded spot area (Spot diameter: 10× Genomics Visium: 55 μm, Nanostring GeoMx DSP: 10 μm [ 7 ], and Slide-seq: 10 μm [ 8 ]) encompasses a diverse population of cells, ranging from a few cells up to 200 cells [ 9 ]. To accurately distinguish the mixed-cell populations and uncover biological inferences from the ST data, it is essential to develop computational models that can enhance the resolution of ST data.  Several computational methods have been developed to improve the spatial resolution of ST data. Bayesian-based methods such as BayesSpace [ 10 ] refine gene expression to sub-spot resolution, only yielding modest improvement. Deep-learning-based approaches such as SPOTlight [ 11 ], Tangram [ 12 ], cell2location [ 13 ], and CARD [ 14 ] integrate ST data with scRNA-seq data, mapping related gene expression cells to ST coordinates or reconstructing the ST landscape from various cell combinations. However, the reliance on scRNA-seq data significantly raises the experimental costs and introduces constraints, including limited cell types and potential biases in spatial reconstruction accuracy.  Instead of relying on the scRNA-seq data, integrating histology images with ST data presents a more feasible and promising way to enhance ST resolution. Most ST platforms, such as Visium and HDST, typically provide corresponding histology images, like hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining images, which offer high-resolution morphological and spatial information for individual cells across the tissue sections. Deep-learning-based methods such as TESLA [ 15 ], XFuse [ 16 ], and iStar [ 17 ] have been developed to integrate the histology image with ST data to enhance ST resolution. However, these methods primarily enhance resolution at the pixel level but fall short of achieving cell-level gene expression resolution. Furthermore, these methods focus on extracting pixel level histological features [e.g. pixel intensities in red, green, blue (RGB) channels], neglecting true cell features and cell–cell interactions, which compromises model accuracy. A specialized model that directly incorporates actual cell-level features is necessary to improve the biological application of ST data.  Many fundamental biological questions—including the delineation of cell-type boundaries, characterization of the tumor microenvironment, and inference of cell–cell communication—inherently require cell-level resolution. However, true single-cell spatial assays such as Xenium or MERFISH remain expensive, limited in gene panel size, and not universally available, making spot-level ST the dominant modality in practice. Moreover, matched scRNA-seq data from the same tissue, which several existing deconvolution methods depend on, is not always obtainable and may introduce additional biases when tissue dissociation alters cell-type composition. A computational approach that can reliably infer cell-level expression directly from spot-level ST data and routine histology images therefore addresses a practical and widely encountered gap in the field.  In this work, we developed an innovative model called DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), which incorporates the cell level features from histology image with ST data using dynamic edge–conditioned graph convolution neural network ( Fig. 1 , and  Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Starting with a histology image, we perform cell segmentation and explicitly extract cell morphological and spatial interaction features, followed by constructing the cellular graphic interaction structures of the tissue. We then build a graph deconvolution model that combines ST data with these morphological features and interaction structures to deconvolute spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression profiles. In contrast to the previous methods that primarily rely on pixel-level information and use convolutional neural network (CNN)-like structures to encode the features, which often failing to capture cell–cell interaction information. DeSpaST leverages the graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to fully capture the cellular interaction topologies by constructing cellular interaction graphic structures. Unlike conventional CNNs, GCNs operate on non-Euclidean data structures, enabling comprehensive modeling of diverse cellular interaction topologies. DeSpaST offers several practical advantages. First, it does not require scRNA-seq references, reducing experimental cost and avoiding dependence on matched dissociated-cell datasets. Second, it leverages morphology and local tissue architecture to improve spatial localization and denoising within spots, which is particularly valuable in heterogeneous tumors where boundaries and niches vary over short distances. Third, DeSpaST’s inferred cell-level expression supports downstream analyses that are difficult at spot resolution, such as cell-type mapping at cellular granularity, spatial domain characterization, and trajectory inference. In our experiments, these advantages manifest as improved agreement with orthogonal measurements (e.g. Xenium), clearer spatial patterns, and improved recovery of spatial domains, with robustness supported by ablations demonstrating that performance depends on both transcriptional input and morphology rather than visual cues alone. Together, these considerations motivate DeSpaST as a practical and interpretable approach for cell-level resolution inference from spot-based ST, while clarifying the conditions under which it is most reliable.    Result   Overview of the DeSpaST model  DeSpaST requires only two inputs: a histology image and ST data ( Fig. 1a ). Histology images offer the individual cell spatial organization and morphology characterization, while the ST data provide gene expression at the spot level. To explicitly extract the cell spatial and organization characterizations from the histology image, we first employed the HD-staining deep-learning algorithm [ 18 ,  19 ] to segment and classify the cell nucleus from the tissue image. Alternatively, other methods for cell or nuclei segmentation could also be applied at this step. We then extracted the morphology features for each cell to construct the cellular graphic structures (see  Fig. 1a  and  Method  section for details). DeSpaST builds the graphic convolution networks by performing the four following steps: (i) extract image patches based on the spot coordinates in the ST data; (ii) construct a directed cellular graphic structure for each patch using nearest neighbors based on the Euclidean distance from a cell to its neighbors; and (iii) derive features from the directed cellular graphic structures to incorporate the spatial and morphology information of the cells into the graph convolutional network. Each node in the graph represents a cell. Node features include cell size, shape, and other morphological features. Edges denote spatial and morphological relationships between cells. Edge features include cell spatial proximity, cell connectivity angle, and interaction edge categorization ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) [ 4 ]. The model is then constructed using two convolutional layers and one fully connected layer ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). All cell nodes are updated through a message passing from all neighboring nodes in each convolutional layer, which incorporates both morphological and cell–cell spatial interaction features of neighboring cells. In this study, we demonstrate DeSpaST’s ability in accurately capturing cell-level gene expression to overcoming spatial resolution limitations in ST data, using breast, lung, and ovarian cancer datasets as examples. DeSpaST offers a new convenient tool for advancing biomedical research, with broad applicability to diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets.    DeSpaST effectively enhances gene expression resolution  To assess the efficacy of DeSpaST, we applied the model to a well-studied breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. We then conducted a comparative analysis of DeSpaST’s performance against the TESLA model [ 15 ], which is a machine-learning framework designed to enhance gene expression to pixel-level resolution [ 15 ]. DeSpaST demonstrated notable advancements in elucidating gene expression patterns. To illustrate, we present two marker genes,  MS4A1  and  ERBB2 , as representative examples ( Fig. 1b ). The  MS4A1  gene encodes the surface molecule CD20, which serves as a widely recognized marker indicative of B-cell lineage [ 21 ].  ERBB2  encodes the human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2) protein [ 22 ], which is used as a tumor marker in breast cancer diagnosis [ 23 ,  24 ]. For each gene, the cell-level gene expression profile from DeSpaST, spot-level gene expression pattern from Visium ST data, and the pixel-level gene expression patterns from TESLA ( Fig. 1b ), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ) were plotted separately. Compared to Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse, DeSpaST showed the gene expression profiles with highest clarity and precision for both genes, successfully enhancing the gene expression resolution. Notably, the gene expression patterns from DeSpaST correlated well with the pathologist-annotated regions. DeSpaST high  ERBB2  gene expression cells closely matched the pathologist-annotated tumor regions. Also, the DeSpaST high  MS4A1  expressed cells were well aligned with the annotated immune cell regions. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse did not achieve the same level of visual clarity as DeSpaST in these regions. The  MS4A1  gene expression profile is particularly noteworthy because it is nearly imperceptible in the Visium ST data and in the reconstructions produced by TESLA ( Fig. 1b , right), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3b ), whereas DeSpaST accurately discerns the  MS4A1  gene expression pattern and immune cell regions.  Remarkably, DeSpaST’s cell-level gene expression predictions demonstrate its capability and reliability in distinguishing between different cell layers. In three specific areas ( Fig. 1c  and  d , and  Supplementary Fig. S4 ), pathologists meticulously annotated the invasive carcinoma and immune cell regions to delineate their boundaries in the H&E images. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST effectively differentiated between these immune cell and tumor cell regions. DeSpaST accurately captured the elevated expression of ERBB2 in tumor regions and the elevated expression of MS4A1 in immune cell regions. The distinct gene expression patterns of MS4A1 and ERBB2 predicted by DeSpaST ( Fig. 1c  and  d  ,  and  Supplementary Fig. S4b ) precisely delineated the tumor and immune boundaries. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse could not accurately delineate these cell layers and boundaries ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ); instead, they only provided ambiguous patterns, which indicates a lack of precision in defining the regions. Moreover, as shown in  Supplementary Fig. S4c , DeSpaST demonstrated exceptional potential in precise cell type annotation. Beyond the highly expressed ERBB2 tumor region, DeSpaST identified an additional layer outside the tumor region with abundant MS4A1 expression, which had not been previously annotated. Upon closer examination of the H&E image by the pathologist, the layer was found to be a lightly stained layer, containing fibrous connective tissues interspersed with inflammatory cells, crucial for restricting tumor expansion. This finding of interspersed immune cells is consistent with the MS4A1 gene expression pattern predicted by DeSpaST.    DeSpaST accurately predicts cellular-level gene expression  The above comparison between pathology annotation and DeSpaST highlights the resolution enhancement power of DeSpaST. To further evaluate the model’s performance, we conducted a direct and comprehensive comparison of cellular-level expression for individual genes. In addition to the Visium spot-level gene expression measurement, Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] also measured the cellular-level gene expression of hundreds of genes through the Xenium experiment. We applied DeSpaST to this breast cancer Visium dataset from Janesick  et al . [ 25 ], segmented and classified the cell nucleus from the H&E image ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), and deconvolving spot-level ST signals into cell-level gene expression profiles. Despite the inherent limitations of adjacent-section comparisons (e.g. local distortion, cell displacement, and microenvironmental differences), DeSpaST showed strong concordance with Xenium in spatial distribution patterns. For example, for the breast cancer marker gene  CCND1  [ 26 ,  27 ] ( Fig. 2a ) and T-cell marker gene  CD69  [ 28 ,  29 ] ( Fig. 2b ), DeSpaST accurately predicted the gene expression patterns, in agreement with the observed patterns in the Xenium. Both Visium and TESLA failed to resolve these patterns adequately, especially in the complex tissue regions. Consider the top of the tissue section ( Fig. 2c  and  Supplementary Fig. S6a ) where intricate tumor and immune cell domains are present. Only DeSpaST successfully captured gene expression within intricate microenvironments ( Fig. 2d  and  e ), accurately reflecting the patterns observed in the Xenium experiment. Conversely, TESLA and Visium failed to capture these spatial variations in gene expression, resulting in unclear expression patterns. In the case of the  CD69  gene ( Fig. 2b ), the Visium ST data are noisy and lack a clear expression pattern. Although TESLA reduces some noise, it fails to capture the inherent gene expression patterns accurately. In contrast, DeSpaST effectively eliminates noise and accurately discerns the true gene expression pattern.    Figure 2   Evaluation of DeSpaST in cell-level gene expression prediction. With the gene pattern identified by DeSpaST, our next step involves a quantitative assessment of the performance enhancement achieved by the DeSpaST model. To facilitate this assessment, spot-level gene expression was reconstructed by taking the average expression of cells inside each spot. For quantitative comparison across methods, we reconstructed spot-level expression by averaging the predicted cellular expressions within each Visium spot and then computed gene-wise Pearson correlations against Xenium for DeSpaST, raw Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DeSpaST exhibits a stronger correlation to Xenium ( r  = 0.754 for  CCND1  gene and  r  = 0.665 for  CD69  gene) than both Visium ( r  = 0.477 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.239 for  CD69  gene) and TESLA ( r  = 0.720 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.424 for  CD69  gene) ( Fig. 2f  and  Supplementary Fig. S3c ). Similar enhancements in clarity and noise reduction in gene expression patterns were observed in other genes as well, such as the  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  genes ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ). DeSpaST demonstrated strong consistency with Xenium experiments for both of these genes, achieving a correlation of  r  = 0.850 for the  ERBB2  gene and  r  = 0.610 for the  MS4A1  gene ( Supplementary Fig. S7c  and  d ). In addition to the above genes, to assess transcriptome-wide generalizability, we computed spot-level Pearson correlations for all examined Xenium genes and summarize the overall trend using correlation density plots ( Fig. 2g ;  Supplementary Fig. S3c ): DeSpaST achieves higher overall agreement with Xenium (median  r  = 0.518) than Visium (median  r  = 0.198) and TESLA (median  r  = 0.479), and the top 20% highest-density region summary consistently favors DeSpaST, indicating systematic improvement beyond a small set of marker genes.  To address the concern that histology-guided models might rely on visual cues and to validate key graph-construction hyperparameters, we performed a comprehensive set of ablation and sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). First, randomizing the input transcriptional counts (“Random count”) caused a substantial collapse in performance—gene-wise correlation with Xenium dropped (CD69:  r  = 0.188; CCND1:  r  = 0.379), the overall summary decreased (top 20% high-density mean correlation: 0.174), and downstream spatial domain agreement deteriorated (NMI: 0.033; ARI: 0.0196)—demonstrating that accurate transcriptional signals are essential and that morphology alone cannot recover meaningful spatial expression. Second, randomizing morphology features (“Random image info”) also reduced performance relative to the full model (e.g. CD69:  r  = 0.423 versus 0.665; top 20% high-density mean: 0.202 versus 0.582; NMI: 0.169 versus 0.194; ARI: 0.0910 versus 0.1167), indicating that morphology provides complementary information but is not solely responsible for DeSpaST’s gains. Finally, we evaluated the robustness of the k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) cell-graph parameter by varying        on the breast dataset: extreme values were suboptimal (e.g. top-20%-density mean correlation = 0.161 at        and 0.220 at       ), while intermediate values (      –12) consistently achieved higher performance (0.58–0.64) and stable domain-detection agreement, supporting our choice of        as a balance between locality and connectivity ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). Together, these analyses show that DeSpaST integrates both transcriptional and morphological information and that its performance is stable across a biologically reasonable range of neighborhood sizes.  To further test whether the deconvoluted outputs preserve biologically meaningful spatial structure beyond individual marker genes, we evaluated each method using a downstream spatial domain detection task on the breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. As shown in ( Supplementary Fig. S9 ), we used the manually annotated domains as ground-truth labels. For each tool, we took the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as input, constructed (i) an expression kNN graph in PCA space and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in 2D coordinate space, fused them into a hybrid connectivity matrix, and inferred domains using Leiden community detection (parameters reported in Supplementary Information). We then quantified concordance with manual annotations using NMI and ARI ( Supplementary Fig. S9b ; higher is better). DeSpaST achieved the best agreement with manual labels (NMI = 0.194; ARI = 0.117), outperforming iStar (NMI = 0.182; ARI = 0.056), XFuse (NMI = 0.033; ARI = 0.011), and TESLA (NMI = 0.143; ARI = 0.031), indicating that DeSpaST’s deconvolution better preserves domain-level organization for downstream spatial analyses.  Supplementary Fig. S9c  further visualizes the inferred domains from each method, where DeSpaST produces domain boundaries that are qualitatively more consistent with the expert annotations.  The remarkable cell-level resolution achieved by DeSpaST creates new possibilities for examining cell–cell communications within a spatial context. For instance, within the cellular milieu surrounding the breast ducts ( Supplementary Fig. S10 ), we detected elevated expressions of breast cancer marker genes  CCND1  and  ERBB2  ( Supplementary Fig. S10a  and  c ). In contrast, immune cell marker genes  CD69  and  MS4A1  ( Supplementary Fig. S10b  and  d ) exhibited high expression in the outside layer adjacent to the tumor cells. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST align with the Xenium gene panel, while TESLA failed to predict them accurately. DeSpaST’s findings suggest possible interactions between immune and tumor cells, highlighting its potential for further studies on the tissue microenvironment and cell–cell communication.    DeSpaST accurately captures the cell-level protein expression  As products of gene expression, protein expressions are generally correlated with differentially expressed mRNAs [ 30 ,  31 ]. Next, we evaluate whether the gene expression patterns obtained by DeSpaST could reflect protein expressions at the cell level [ 25 ]. We plotted and compared the  MS4A1  and  ERBB2  gene expression patterns with the corresponding HER2 and CD20 protein immunofluorescence (IF) signals ( Fig. 3a  and  b ). Interestingly, the gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST closely align with protein expression profiles, while Visium and TESLA are not able to capture them. We calculated the correlations between predicted  MS4A1  gene expression and Xenium IF CD20 protein signals. DeSpaST exhibits superior performance compared to TESLA and Visium with higher correlation ( r  = 0.622 for DeSpaST versus  r  = 0.420 for Visium and  r  = 0.401 for TESLA;  Fig. 3c ). DeSpaST also demonstrated a notably higher correlation of ERBB2 gene expression with HER2 protein expression ( r  = 0.839) when compared to Visium ( r  = 0.821) and TESLA ( r  = 0.660), as illustrated in  Fig. 3d . Although Visium and TESLA also showed good correlations with the HER2 IF signals, DeSpaST significantly outperformed them in predicting fine-grained details gene expression patterns ( Supplementary Fig. S11 ). Notably, only DeSpaST accurately captured the comprehensive pattern of ERBB2 gene expression, depicting the tumor’s shape around the breast duct in alignment with IF protein signals. In contrast, Visium and TESLA predicted a vague outline of ERBB2 expression, lacking finer details and failing to depict a clear pattern. Application of DeSpaST for cell type identification  Given the highly precise cell-level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST, we employed DeSpaST for downstream analysis. This involved leveraging the predicted cell-level gene expression to delineate the spatial distribution of various cell types. Unlike ST data, where one spot may contain multiple cells, DeSpaST’s cellular-level resolution offers a superior depiction of cell-type distribution. Utilizing DeSpaST’s gene expression predictions as input, we applied the cell-type identification algorithm ScType [ 32 ] to assign the cell type to each single cell. The resulting cell-type profiles were mapped back onto the spatial location and detected locations for tumor cells, lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages ( Supplementary Fig. S12a ). To validate the cell-type distribution by DeSpaST, we implemented the ScType algorithm with the Xenium data and plotted the cell-type distribution in  Supplementary Fig. S12b . The spatial distributions of annotated cell types from DeSpaST closely resemble the cell types obtained from Xenium, which further substantiate the accuracy of DeSpaST. To reveal the tumor’s immunological response, we specifically focus on tumor cells and immune cells ( Fig. 4a  and  b ). Both DeSpaST ( Fig. 4a ) and Xenium panel ( Fig. 4b ) delineated similar tumor and immune cell regions. Heterogeneous areas are found at the upper and middle portion of the tissue where tumor and immune cells closely interact, which indicates the recognition and attack of activated immune cells that impede tumor spread. In contrast, tumor regions at the lower portion of the slides appear less confined, forming dense and more aggressive tumor areas where there is a lack of immune cell control. Both Xenium and DeSpaST accurately classify these complex cell environments. While Xenium served as a valuable reference here, DeSpaST exhibits greater potential and offers the flexibility to include more marker genes for cell type classification analysis. Unlike Xenium's panel of 306 genes, DeSpaST can leverage the transcriptomic level gene expression data from ST data. This enables the inclusion of a wider range of cell-type markers, leading to more accurate classification.    Figure 4   Application of DeSpaST in spatial cell-level downstream analysis. Application of DeSpaST in uncovering pseudo temporal trajectories of tumor progression  Following the annotation of cancer cells, we calculated the pseudo-trajectories timeline of tumor development based on the inferred cell level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST. The partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) method was used to construct the topological graph and a cluster with high expression of cancer stem cell marker  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ] was selected as the root node ( Supplementary Fig. S13 ). Pseudotime values were estimated and mapped back to each cell's spatial location to infer the dynamic trajectories of tumor progression ( Fig. 4c ). Interestingly, the clusters of early pseudotime cancer cells and late pseudotime cancer cells occupy markedly distinct regions in the tissue section. These distributions align precisely with the DCIS (ductal carcinoma  in situ ) and invasive tumor regions annotated by expert pathologists ( Fig. 4d ). Tumor cells with early pseudotime exhibit a denser and more uniform composition characterized with reduced variability in size and shape, corresponding to DCIS regions ( Fig. 4d ). In contrast, late pseudotime tumor cells, located in the invasive tumor region, show increased invasivenexss and a more loosely organized structure. Similar cell-level resolution improvement of DeSpaST is also observed in the human lung cancer Visium dataset ( Supplementary Fig. S16 ). We illustrated three marker genes as examples of the resolution improvement compared to the Visium spot level resolution ( Supplementary Fig. S17 ): cancer marker gene  EGFR  [ 39 ], T lymphocyte marker  CD4  [ 40 ], and fibroblast maker  SFRP2  [ 41 ].
